For a sequence $x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ the partial sums are $s_N := \sum_{k<N} x_k$ (the finite sum in the vector space $\mathbb{R}^n$, which is the pointwise finite sum of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 1 -- cite it rather than minting a third finite sum), and $\sum x_k$ CONVERGES to $s$ when $s_N \to s$ in $(\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]); it converges ABSOLUTELY when the real series $\sum\lVert x_k\rVert_2$ converges ([[def-series]]). A REARRANGEMENT is $\sum x_{\sigma(k)}$ for a bijection $\sigma : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, verbatim as in the published [[def-rearrangement-and-unconditional-convergence]]; the SET OF REARRANGEMENT SUMS is $\mathcal{S}(x) := \{\,s : \text{some rearrangement converges to } s\,\}$. AGREEMENT CLAUSE, mandatory: at $n = 1$, under the identification of $\mathbb{R}^1$ with $\mathbb{R}$, these are exactly [[def-series]] and [[def-rearrangement-and-unconditional-convergence]] and $\mathcal{S}$ is exactly the set the published [[rem-rearrangement-in-higher-dimensions]] calls $\mathcal{S}(a)$; state the identification, since $\mathbb{R}^1$ is a function space and not literally $\mathbb{R}$. Everything here needs $n \ge 1$ because $d_2$ does.

items.title: An absolutely convergent series in $\mathbb{R}^n$ converges, and every rearrangement converges to the same sum
items.strategy: direct, in two clauses, both by reduction to the published one-dimensional theory rather than by re-running its proofs. Clause 1: absolute convergence gives a Cauchy sequence of partial sums, by the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]) and the Cauchy criterion for the real series [[thm-series-cauchy-criterion]]; then completeness ([[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]]) gives convergence. Clause 2: each coordinate series converges absolutely because $\lvert (x_k)_i\rvert \le \lVert x_k\rVert_2$ and [[thm-direct-comparison-test]], so [[thm-dirichlet-rearrangement]] applies coordinatewise, and [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]] reassembles the sum. State the consequence in the form the next items use: if $\sum x_k$ converges absolutely then $\mathcal{S}(x)$ is the single point $\{\sum x_k\}$. Note that [[lem-absolute-convergence-implies-convergence]] is the published one-dimensional statement and that this theorem is its $\mathbb{R}^n$ analogue, NOT a generalisation of its proof.

items.title: The subspace $\Gamma$ of directions along which a series converges absolutely, and its orthogonal complement $\Gamma^{\perp}$
items.strategy: definition, PHRASED WITH THE INNER PRODUCT AND NOT WITH LINEAR FUNCTIONALS, and that is a deliberate design decision forced by plan order: the page that introduces linear maps and dual spaces sits earlier in plan order but is not built, so no linear-map vocabulary is available here. For a convergent series $\sum x_k$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ set $\Gamma := \{\,a \in \mathbb{R}^n : \sum_k \lvert\langle a, x_k\rangle\rvert \text{ converges}\,\}$ and $\Gamma^{\perp} := \{\,y \in \mathbb{R}^n : \langle a,y\rangle = 0 \text{ for every } a \in \Gamma\,\}$. PROVE BOTH ARE LINEAR SUBSPACES ([[def-linear-subspace]], [[lem-linear-subspace-criterion]]): for $\Gamma$ use bilinearity and [[lem-series-linearity]] with [[thm-direct-comparison-test]]; for $\Gamma^{\perp}$ use bilinearity alone. Record $0 \in \Gamma$ always, and $\Gamma = \mathbb{R}^n$ exactly when the series converges absolutely (one direction by comparison with $\lVert x_k\rVert_2$ using [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], the other by testing against the standard basis and [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]'s comparison chain) -- that equivalence is what makes the next theorem contain [[thm-absolute-convergence-in-rn]] as a special case. Define AFFINE SUBSPACE as a coset $s + W$ of a linear subspace, since the library has no such notion yet, and prove the coset is determined by $W$ and any of its points.

items.title: Steinitz's polygonal confinement theorem: finitely many vectors of norm at most $1$ summing to $0$ can be ordered so that every partial sum has norm at most $n$
items.strategy: constructive, and the proof is fully available from published material; scaffold it in five named stages and check each. STATEMENT: let $n \ge 1$, let $v : m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with $\lVert v_i\rVert_2 \le 1$ for every $i<m$ and $\sum_{i<m} v_i = 0$; then there is a bijection $\pi : m \to m$ with $\lVert\sum_{i<k} v_{\pi(i)}\rVert_2 \le \iota(n)$ for every $k \le m$. (1) If $m \le n$ every partial sum has norm at most $\iota(k) \le \iota(n)$ by the triangle inequality; assume $m > n$. (2) For $n \le k \le m$ let $\Lambda_k := \{\lambda : m \to [0,1] \mid \sum_i \lambda_i v_i = 0,\ \sum_i \lambda_i = \iota(k-n)\}$ RELATIVE TO A SUBSET $A_k$ (see 3). $\Lambda_m$ contains the constant $\iota(m-n)/\iota(m)$, since $\sum v_i = 0$. (3) DESCENDING CONSTRUCTION: build $A_m \supseteq A_{m-1} \supseteq \dots \supseteq A_n$ with $\lvert A_k\rvert = k$ and $\lambda^{k}$ supported in $A_k$, in $[0,1]^{A_k}$, with $\sum_{i \in A_k}\lambda^k_i v_i = 0$ and $\sum_{i\in A_k}\lambda^k_i = \iota(k-n)$. Given $A_k,\lambda^k$, the feasible set for $k-1$ is nonempty (scale $\lambda^k$ by $\iota(k-1-n)/\iota(k-n)$; the case $k-n = 0$ does not arise since the construction stops at $k = n$). (4) THE KEY LEMMA, and it is pure linear algebra: among the feasible $\lambda$ choose one with the FEWEST coordinates in the open interval $(0,1)$ -- legitimate because a nonempty set of naturals has a least element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]). If that number were at least $n+2$, the vectors $(v_i,1) \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ indexed by the fractional coordinates would be more than $\dim \mathbb{R}^{n+1} = n+1$ in number, hence linearly dependent ([[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[def-dimension]]); a nontrivial dependence $\mu$ gives $\sum\mu_i v_i = 0$ and $\sum\mu_i = 0$, and moving $\lambda + t\mu$ to the nearest $t$ at which some fractional coordinate reaches $0$ or $1$ (a minimum over a nonempty finite set of reals, [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]) keeps feasibility and strictly reduces the count -- contradiction. So at most $n+1$ coordinates are fractional. (5) THE SUPPORT BOUND, the step that makes the nesting work and the one an inattentive proof omits: $\#\{i : \lambda_i = 1\} \le \sum_i\lambda_i = k-1-n$, so $\#\mathrm{supp}(\lambda) \le (k-1-n)+(n+1) = k$; and equality would force the fractional coordinates to sum to $0$ while each is strictly positive, which is impossible, so $\#\mathrm{supp}(\lambda) \le k-1$ and an $A_{k-1} \subseteq A_k$ of size $k-1$ containing the support exists. (6) THE ORDERING: enumerate $A_n$ first in any order, then the single element of $A_{k}\setminus A_{k-1}$ for $k = n+1,\dots,m$ in increasing $k$. For $k \le n$ the partial sum has norm at most $\iota(k)\le\iota(n)$; for $k \ge n$ the partial sum is $\sum_{i\in A_k} v_i = \sum_{i\in A_k}(1-\lambda^k_i)v_i$, whose norm is at most $\sum_{i\in A_k}(1-\lambda^k_i) = \iota(k) - \iota(k-n) = \iota(n)$. Every sum here is a sum over a finite index set; if the counting page's index-set sum is not among this page's declared prerequisites, index by a chosen enumeration and use [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] instead. LANDMARK.

items.title: The set of rearrangement sums of a convergent series in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a nonempty subset of the affine subspace $s + \Gamma^{\perp}$
items.strategy: direct, and it is the containment half of the Levy-Steinitz theorem; SCOPE THE CLAIM EXACTLY AND DO NOT OVERSTATE THE TITLE, since a title claiming more than the proof gives is a fatal defect. Let $\sum x_k$ converge to $s$. Nonemptiness: $s \in \mathcal{S}(x)$, via the identity bijection. Containment: let $t \in \mathcal{S}(x)$, so $\sum x_{\sigma(k)} = t$ for some bijection $\sigma$, and let $a \in \Gamma$. The real series $\sum\langle a,x_k\rangle$ converges absolutely by definition of $\Gamma$, so by the published [[thm-dirichlet-rearrangement]] every rearrangement of it has the same sum; and $\langle a,\cdot\rangle$ is continuous ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]], or directly by Cauchy-Schwarz) and additive on finite sums ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 1), so $\langle a,t\rangle = \sum_k\langle a,x_{\sigma(k)}\rangle = \sum_k\langle a,x_k\rangle = \langle a,s\rangle$. Hence $\langle a, t-s\rangle = 0$ for every $a \in \Gamma$, that is $t - s \in \Gamma^{\perp}$. State the two extreme cases as clauses, because they are exactly the published one-dimensional dichotomy seen from here: if the series converges absolutely then $\Gamma = \mathbb{R}^n$, $\Gamma^{\perp} = \{0\}$ and $\mathcal{S}(x) = \{s\}$ ([[thm-absolute-convergence-in-rn]]); at $n = 1$ a conditionally convergent series has $\Gamma = \{0\}$ and $\Gamma^{\perp} = \mathbb{R}$, and the published [[thm-riemann-series-theorem]] says the containment is then an EQUALITY. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED, and must be said in Remarks in exactly these terms: this theorem gives containment only; whether $\mathcal{S}(x)$ is all of $s+\Gamma^{\perp}$ for $n \ge 2$ is not settled here, and no assertion about it, in either direction, is made anywhere on this page. Declare [[rem-rearrangement-in-higher-dimensions]] nowhere in `deps` -- it is a published remark on an earlier page and the edge runs the other way, as a forward reference to be added there. LANDMARK.

items.title: Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order
items.strategy: the page ledger, and on this page it carries more weight than usual because three separate scope decisions were taken. Record: (1) THE $n \ge 1$ HYPOTHESIS, where it comes from ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $d_\infty$ only there) and exactly which items inherit it -- list them; note that [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the vector space structure are fine at $n = 0$, so the boundary is between the algebra and the metric, not between statements a reader would guess. (2) THE EXPONENT IN $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ IS RATIONAL, because real exponents do not exist at this point in the reading order ([[rem-real-exponents-deferred]]); every $p$-norm statement on this page carries it. (3) $\mathbb{R}^n$ IS A FUNCTION SPACE, the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-function-space]]), so $\mathbb{R}^1$ is not literally $\mathbb{R}$ and every comparison with the one-dimensional theory goes through the stated identification. (4) WHAT IS TAKEN UP ELSEWHERE, phrased as reading order and never as a claim about the library as a whole: the operator norm and the fact that linear maps are Lipschitz belong with linear maps, which are introduced on a page earlier in plan order that is not yet built; the general theory of inner product spaces and orthogonality likewise; uniform convergence, the total derivative and the integral in $\mathbb{R}^m$ all come later in this track. (5) THE OPEN HALF OF THE REARRANGEMENT QUESTION: [[thm-rearrangement-sums-lie-in-an-affine-subspace]] proves containment and the page asserts nothing about the reverse inclusion for $n \ge 2$; the published [[rem-rearrangement-in-higher-dimensions]] on the series page raised the question and this page answers the part it can. State that plainly; do NOT state the classical answer, in any form, and do not create a recorded-not-proved item for it.

pages.title: R^n as a Normed Space; Vector-Valued Functions: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $f(t) = (t^{2}, t^{3})$ on $[0,1]$: no $\xi$ satisfies $f(1)-f(0) = f'(\xi)$
items.strategy: counterexample, refuting the equality form of the mean value theorem for $m \ge 2$ and confirming that [[thm-mean-value-inequality]] is the correct statement. $f(1)-f(0) = (1,1)$ and $f'(t) = (2t,3t^{2})$ ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]] componentwise, via [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); $2\xi = 1$ forces $\xi = 1/\iota(2)$, and then $3\xi^{2} = 3/\iota(4) \ne 1$. Do the arithmetic in $\mathbb{R}$ with the canonical naturals visible. CHOSEN DELIBERATELY OVER THE CLASSICAL WITNESS: the crispest classical example is $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$ on $[0,2\pi]$, and the trigonometric functions are introduced later in the reading order, so a polynomial curve is used instead; record that substitution here rather than in a scaffold note, since a reader who knows the classical example will look for it. Then CHECK the inequality form on the same curve: $\lVert f(1)-f(0)\rVert_2 = \sqrt{2}$ and $\sup\lVert f'\rVert_2 = \sqrt{13}$ on $[0,1]$, so the inequality holds with room to spare.

items.title: The comparison constants between $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$, and vectors attaining each
items.strategy: computation, and the value is that every constant is shown SHARP by an attaining vector, which the general theorem [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] does not supply. On $\mathbb{R}^{2}$: $\lVert x\rVert_\infty \le \lVert x\rVert_2 \le \lVert x\rVert_1 \le \iota(2)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ and $\lVert x\rVert_1 \le \sqrt{2}\lVert x\rVert_2$; exhibit $e_0$ (attaining the first, third-from-left and the outer chain at one end) and $(1,1)$ (attaining $\lVert x\rVert_1 = 2$, $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \sqrt{2}$, $\lVert x\rVert_\infty = 1$, which is the extreme case of both the $\sqrt{2}$ and the $\iota(2)$ constants). Verify each inequality from [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]'s chain and [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]]. Also compute the unit balls' inclusions to make the geometry explicit.

items.title: $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ violates the parallelogram law, so no symmetric bilinear form induces it
items.strategy: counterexample with a two-line computation and a precise conclusion. Take $x = e_0$, $y = e_1$: $\lVert x+y\rVert_1^{2}+\lVert x-y\rVert_1^{2} = 4+4 = 8$ while $2\lVert x\rVert_1^{2}+2\lVert y\rVert_1^{2} = 4$. Since every norm arising from an inner product satisfies the parallelogram law ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] clause (b)), no inner product on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ induces $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$. STATE THE LOGIC PRECISELY: the page proves the parallelogram law only for the Euclidean inner product, so the conclusion available here is about norms of that form; a general converse (the Jordan-von Neumann theorem, that the parallelogram law characterises inner-product norms) is not proved on this page and must not be asserted. Note also that $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$ IS equivalent to $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ by [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] -- equivalence of norms is a metric statement and says nothing about inner products, which is the point worth making.

items.title: $g(x,y) = xy/(x^{2}+y^{2})$, extended by $g(0,0)=0$, is continuous in each variable separately and not continuous at the origin
items.strategy: counterexample. Continuity in each variable separately at the origin: $g(x,0) = 0$ and $g(0,y) = 0$ for all $x,y$, so both partial functions are constant. Discontinuity at the origin: along the line $y = x$ the value is $1/\iota(2)$ for $x \ne 0$, and points of that line come arbitrarily close to the origin, so no $\delta$ works ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]], [[def-metric-continuity]]); or use the sequential criterion with $(1/\iota(k+1), 1/\iota(k+1))$ and [[thm-metric-continuity-characterisations]]. Continuity away from the origin follows from [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]] and [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]. THE POINT IS THAT SEPARATE CONTINUITY IS STRICTLY WEAKER, and this is the first place in the library where a function of several real variables appears, so state the domain as $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with the metric of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] rather than informally.

items.title: A convergent sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and the integral $\int_0^1 (1, t, t^{2})$, computed componentwise
items.strategy: computation exercising both halves of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] and [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]]. Take $x^{(k)} = (1/\iota(k+1),\ 1 - 1/\iota(k+1),\ 2)$ and show $x^{(k)} \to (0,1,2)$ by the componentwise criterion, checking that the $\varepsilon$ for the vector is obtained from the three coordinate $\varepsilon$'s exactly as the theorem's proof does. Then compute $\int_0^1 (1,t,t^{2}) = (1, 1/\iota(2), 1/\iota(3))$ by [[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]] componentwise, and CHECK the norm inequality [[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]] on this example numerically: $\lVert\int f\rVert_2$ against $\int\lVert f\rVert_2$, bounding the latter from below by a crude estimate rather than evaluating it, since its exact value needs machinery not available here. Say that the inequality is strict here and why.

items.title: Steinitz's confinement bound realised on an explicit list of six unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ summing to zero
items.strategy: verification, and it makes an abstract existence proof concrete. Take six vectors of norm at most $1$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ summing to $0$ -- for instance $\pm e_0, \pm e_1$ together with $\pm(1,1)/\sqrt{2}$ -- exhibit an ordering whose partial sums all have norm at most $\iota(2)$, and exhibit a BAD ordering whose partial sums exceed $1$, so that the theorem is seen to say something. Then trace one step of the descending construction of [[thm-steinitz-polygonal-confinement]] on this list: write down $A_6$, one $\lambda^{6}$, and the resulting $A_5$, checking the support bound $\#\mathrm{supp} \le k-1$ that the proof turns on. An example that only asserts the bound would be worth much less than one that exhibits the construction.

items.title: A convergent series in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with $\Gamma$ a line and $\Gamma^{\perp}$ a line, computed from the definition
items.strategy: computation, and it is the example that makes [[def-the-space-of-summing-directions]] concrete. Take $x_k := \bigl((-1)^{k}/\iota(k+1),\ 0\bigr)$: the series converges by the alternating series test ([[thm-alternating-series-test]]) in the first coordinate and trivially in the second. For $a = (a_0,a_1)$, $\langle a,x_k\rangle = a_0(-1)^{k}/\iota(k+1)$, so $\sum\lvert\langle a,x_k\rangle\rvert$ converges iff $a_0 = 0$ (harmonic divergence, [[thm-p-series-rational]] at $p=1$ or [[thm-cauchy-condensation]]). Hence $\Gamma = \{(0,a_1)\}$, a line, and $\Gamma^{\perp} = \{(y_0,0)\}$, a line. So [[thm-rearrangement-sums-lie-in-an-affine-subspace]] confines every rearrangement sum to the horizontal line through $s$ -- and, since the second coordinate is identically $0$, that confinement is visibly sharp in the trivial direction. Note what this example does NOT decide: whether every point of that line is attained. Say so; do not assert it.

items.title: FALSE: if a convergent series in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ does not converge absolutely, then every point of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the sum of some rearrangement of it
items.strategy: refutation, and it is the item that stops a reader generalising [[thm-riemann-series-theorem]] by analogy -- the exact expectation the published [[rem-rearrangement-in-higher-dimensions]] warns against. Use the series of [[ex-gamma-and-its-complement-computed-for-a-plane-series]]: it converges, it does not converge absolutely (its norms are $1/\iota(k+1)$, whose series diverges), and every rearrangement has second coordinate $0$, so no point off the horizontal line through $s$ is a rearrangement sum. That refutes the statement without needing any part of the classical higher-dimensional theorem, which is the point: the refutation is elementary and complete. Note that [[thm-rearrangement-sums-lie-in-an-affine-subspace]] explains it structurally, $\Gamma^{\perp}$ being a proper subspace, and that the one-dimensional case is genuinely different because there $\Gamma = \{0\}$ forces $\Gamma^{\perp} = \mathbb{R}$.

items.title: FALSE: all norms on a real vector space are equivalent
items.strategy: refutation on an infinite-dimensional space built from published material only. Let $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of sequences with only finitely many nonzero terms; it is a linear subspace of the function space $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ ([[def-function-space]], [[lem-linear-subspace-criterion]]) -- prove that, it is two lines. On $V$ define $N_1(v) := \sum_{k<K}\lvert v_k\rvert$ for any $K$ beyond the last nonzero index (well defined: prove the value does not depend on $K$, which is where finiteness of the support is spent) and $N_\infty(v) := \max\{\lvert v_k\rvert : k<K\}$; both are norms by the same computations as [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]. The vectors $u^{(m)} := e_0+\dots+e_{m-1}$ have $N_1(u^{(m)}) = \iota(m)$ and $N_\infty(u^{(m)}) = 1$, so no constant $C$ satisfies $N_1 \le C N_\infty$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]). STATE THE HYPOTHESIS THAT FAILS: [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] is about $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n$ a natural number, and its proof spends compactness of the unit sphere, which is a finite-dimensional fact; $V$ is not finite-dimensional ([[def-dimension]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] give the comparison). Do not claim anything about general infinite-dimensional normed spaces, a theory this library has not built.

items.title: FALSE: in every normed space a closed bounded set is compact
items.strategy: refutation on the same space $V$ of finitely supported sequences used in the previous item, with the norm $N_\infty$. The closed unit ball of $(V,N_\infty)$ is closed and bounded ([[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) but not compact: the standard unit vectors $e_k$ all lie in it and satisfy $N_\infty(e_j - e_k) = 1$ for $j \ne k$, so no subsequence is Cauchy ([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]) and none converges, contradicting sequential compactness ([[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]], [[def-metric-compactness-variants]]). STATE WHERE THE PUBLISHED THEOREM'S HYPOTHESIS IS: [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is about $\mathbb{R}^n$ for a natural $n$, and its bisection proof consumes exactly that finiteness. Note as a bonus that the same family shows $(V,N_\infty)$ is not totally bounded ([[def-totally-bounded]]), which is the property the general metric characterisation [[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] identifies as missing.

items.title: FALSE: a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose coordinate sequences are each bounded converges
items.strategy: refutation by the smallest possible witness, and it is here to separate two statements that are easy to conflate. Take $n = 1$ and the sequence $x^{(k)} = ((-1)^{k})$: each coordinate is bounded, and the sequence does not converge ([[lem-limit-unique]] with two subsequential limits, or [[thm-convergence-iff-limsup-equals-liminf]]). The TRUE statement in the neighbourhood is [[cor-bolzano-weierstrass-in-rn]]: a bounded sequence has a convergent SUBSEQUENCE, not a limit. Also state the true componentwise statement, [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]] clause 1, which is about convergence and not about boundedness, and point out that the false statement conflates the hypothesis of one with the conclusion of the other.

items.title: A curve for which the mean value inequality is an equality, showing the constant cannot be improved
items.strategy: the positive companion of the first item on this page, and it is what makes [[thm-mean-value-inequality]] sharp rather than merely true. Take $f(t) = (t, 0)$ on $[0,1]$: $\lVert f'\rVert_2 \equiv 1$ and $\lVert f(1)-f(0)\rVert_2 = 1 = 1\cdot(1-0)$. So no constant smaller than $\sup\lVert f'\rVert_2$ works in general, and the inequality is the best possible statement of its shape. Contrast with the first item on this page, where the same inequality is strict; the two together show that the failure of the equality FORM is not a failure of the bound. Compute both norms explicitly.

pages.title: Sequences and Series of Functions; Uniform Convergence

items.title: Pointwise convergence, uniform convergence, and the uniformly Cauchy condition for sequences of real-valued functions
Uniform convergence of real-valued functions implies pointwise convergence
A sequence of real-valued functions converges uniformly if and only if it is uniformly Cauchy
A series of real-valued functions and its pointwise and uniform convergence through its partial sums
A series of real-valued functions converges uniformly if and only if its tails are uniformly small
Uniform limits respect sums and scalar multiples
Products converge uniformly when both factors converge uniformly and one limiting factor and one approximating family are uniformly bounded
The uniform limit of continuous real-valued functions on a metric space is continuous
The uniform limit of uniformly continuous real-valued functions is uniformly continuous
The space $C(K,\mathbb{R})$ of continuous real-valued functions on a nonempty compact metric space
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is complete in the supremum metric for every nonempty compact metric space $K$
Uniformly close integrable functions have integrals differing by at most the interval length times their uniform error
A uniform limit of Riemann-integrable functions is Riemann integrable, and its integral is the limit of their integrals

If continuously differentiable functions converge at one point and their derivatives converge uniformly on a closed interval, then the functions converge uniformly to a differentiable function whose derivative is the derivative limit
The Weierstrass M-test gives absolute pointwise convergence and uniform convergence of a function series
Uniform Dirichlet test: uniformly bounded partial sums times a uniformly decreasing null family give a uniformly convergent function series
Uniform Abel test: a uniformly convergent function series times a uniformly bounded pointwise monotone family gives a uniformly convergent product series
Dini's theorem on a closed interval: monotone pointwise convergence of continuous functions to a continuous limit is uniform
Agreement of the quantified real-valued definition with the later uniform-metric and uniform-topology formulations

pages.title: Sequences and Series of Functions; Uniform Convergence: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $f_k(x)=x^{k+1}$ converges pointwise but not uniformly on $[0,1]$
Shrinking rectangles converge pointwise to zero while every integral equals one
Dini's theorem fails on $[0,\infty)$: $x/(k+1+x)$ decreases pointwise to zero but not uniformly
Dini's theorem fails for discontinuous approximants: shrinking interval indicators decrease pointwise to zero but not uniformly
Dini's theorem fails for a discontinuous limit: powers on $[0,1]$ decrease pointwise to a discontinuous endpoint indicator but not uniformly
Continuous triangular spikes on $[0,1]$ converge pointwise to zero but not uniformly when monotonicity is absent
The double sequence $(m+1)/(m+n+2)$ has unequal iterated limits
$x/(1+(k+1)^2x^2)$ converges uniformly to zero on $\mathbb{R}$ while every derivative at zero equals one

pages.title: Approximation and Compactness in C(K)

items.title: Equicontinuity, pointwise boundedness, and uniform boundedness for families in $C(K,\mathbb R)$
An equicontinuous family on a compact metric space is uniformly equicontinuous
items.strategy: Choose one equicontinuity neighbourhood at each point, extract a finite half-radius cover, and use a triangle estimate through the corresponding centre. Keep the empty family and empty domain explicit.

items.title: Equicontinuity and pointwise boundedness on a compact metric space imply uniform boundedness
items.strategy: Use uniform equicontinuity at tolerance one and a finite cover; combine the finitely many pointwise bounds with the triangle inequality.

items.title: An equicontinuous pointwise-bounded family in $C(K,\mathbb R)$ has a finite net in the supremum metric
items.strategy: Sample on a finite domain net, discretize the bounded sample vectors by a finite grid, and show functions in one grid cell are uniformly close using equicontinuity. Treat the empty family separately.

items.title: A uniformly convergent sequence of continuous functions, together with its limit, is equicontinuous
items.strategy: Control the finite initial segment by intersecting finitely many continuity neighbourhoods and control the tail by two uniform-error terms plus continuity of the limit.

items.title: Arzelà–Ascoli for real $C(K)$: compact closure iff equicontinuous and pointwise bounded
items.strategy: For sufficiency use the finite-sup-net lemma, completeness of $C(K)$, and the metric compactness equivalences. For necessity, compactness gives bounded evaluation images and finite sup nets; use continuity of finitely many centres to recover equicontinuity. Prove both directions and include empty cases.

items.title: Every pointwise-bounded equicontinuous sequence in $C(K,\mathbb R)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence
items.strategy: Apply Arzelà–Ascoli to the range of the sequence and then sequential compactness of its compact closure.

items.title: The Bernstein polynomial $B_n(f)$ on $[0,1]$
The zeroth, first, and second centred moments of the Bernstein basis
items.strategy: Use the binomial theorem and the identities $k{n\choose k}=n{n-1\choose k-1}$ and $k(k-1){n\choose k}=n(n-1){n-2\choose k-2}$, with $n=0,1$ separated before division.

items.title: Bernstein polynomials converge uniformly to every continuous function on $[0,1]$
items.strategy: Use uniform continuity to split the Bernstein average into near and far indices; bound the far mass by the second centred moment. Choose the integer degree after fixing epsilon and keep both endpoints explicit.

items.title: Polynomials are uniformly dense in $C([0,1],\mathbb R)$
items.strategy: Each Bernstein approximant is a polynomial and the preceding theorem supplies uniform convergence.

items.title: Polynomials are uniformly dense in $C([a,b],\mathbb R)$ for every closed interval
items.strategy: For $a<b$, transport the unit-interval approximation by the affine homeomorphism; handle the singleton interval $a=b$ by a constant polynomial.

items.title: A unital point-separating real subalgebra of $C(K,\mathbb R)$
The uniform closure of a unital real function algebra is closed under absolute value, maximum, and minimum
items.strategy: Approximate the absolute-value function uniformly on a large closed interval by polynomials whose constant term is adjusted to zero; substitute a bounded function into those polynomials, then use the algebraic formulas for maximum and minimum.

items.title: A unital separating real function algebra interpolates arbitrary values at two distinct points
items.strategy: Normalize a separating function affinely; the denominator is nonzero because the two sampled values differ. Treat coincident points only when the requested values agree.

items.title: Real Stone–Weierstrass theorem for compact metric spaces
items.strategy: Work in the uniform closure. For each first point, use two-point interpolation and compactness to take a finite maximum dominating the target everywhere while matching at that point; compactness again gives a finite minimum approximating the target uniformly. Invoke the lattice lemma at both stages.

items.title: A complete metric space is not a countable union of closed sets with empty interior
items.strategy: Given nonempty open data, recursively choose nested closed balls with radii tending to zero and each avoiding the next closed set. Dependent choice supplies the sequence; completeness supplies its limit, which lies in the original open set and outside every closed set. Include the empty-space convention.

items.title: Functions satisfying a fixed local Lipschitz bound somewhere form a closed subset of $C([0,1])$
items.strategy: Let a sequence in the fixed pointwise-Lipschitz set converge in the supremum metric. Unwind metric convergence and the supremum bound to obtain uniform convergence, use the earlier real-valued uniform-limit theorem for continuity of the limit, and apply Bolzano-Weierstrass to the witness points in $[0,1]$. Pass the defining inequality to the convergent witness subsequence using uniform convergence and continuity, with the endpoint interpretation explicit.

items.title: Polygonal functions with sufficiently steep nonvertex slopes are dense in $C([0,1])$
items.strategy: Choose a fine uniform partition from uniform continuity, perturb the sampled vertex values by a small alternating sawtooth, and linearly interpolate. Bound the sup error and choose the perturbation frequency so every nonvertex slope has the prescribed magnitude.

items.title: Continuous nowhere differentiable functions form a dense subset of $C([0,1],\mathbb R)$
items.strategy: For each integer bound, show the functions having that local difference-quotient bound somewhere form a closed set with empty interior, using the two preceding lemmas. Apply the locally proved Baire theorem and identify the complement with functions having no finite derivative, using one-sided derivatives at endpoints.

items.title: The tent function $\phi(t)=\operatorname{dist}(t,\mathbb Z)$ and the Takagi series $T(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}2^{-n}\phi(2^n x)$
The Takagi series converges uniformly to a continuous nowhere differentiable function
items.strategy: Apply the M-test using $0\le\phi\le1/2$. On dyadic intervals record the exact integer slopes of partial sums; compare symmetric or one-sided dyadic difference quotients and show they cannot converge to a finite limit, separating dyadic and nondyadic points.

pages.title: Approximation and Compactness in C(K): Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Rudin's bounded rational spikes are not equicontinuous and have no uniformly convergent subsequence
items.strategy: For $f_n(x)=x^2/(x^2+(1-nx)^2)$ on $[0,1]$, verify $0\le f_n\le1$, $f_n(0)=0$, and $f_n(1/n)=1$. This defeats equicontinuity at zero; any uniform subsequential limit would be continuous but must be zero at every positive point and equal one along the moving peaks.

items.title: All constant functions form an equicontinuous family that is not pointwise bounded
items.strategy: Every function difference is zero, so one delta works for the whole family; at any point the values range over all real numbers.

items.title: Translations of a fixed bump on $\mathbb R$ are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous but have no uniformly convergent subsequence
items.strategy: Use the triangular bump $b(x)=\max(1-|x|,0)$ and its integer translates. They share a Lipschitz constant and a uniform bound, while distinct translates with centres separated by at least two have sup distance one; every subsequence contains such a separated pair.

items.title: The Bernstein polynomials of $f(x)=x^2$ equal $x^2+x(1-x)/n$
items.strategy: Use the first two Bernstein moment identities and compute the exact uniform error, including the degree-zero convention separately.

items.title: The family $x\mapsto|x-a|$, $a\in[0,1]$, is compact in $C([0,1])$
items.strategy: The reverse triangle inequality gives a common Lipschitz bound and identifies the sup distance between parameters with $|a-b|$. Apply Arzelà–Ascoli, or directly transport sequential compactness of the parameter interval.

items.title: Even polynomials on $[-1,1]$ form a unital algebra but are not dense because they do not separate $-1$ and $1$
items.strategy: Uniform limits preserve equality at the two endpoints, whereas the identity function has unequal endpoint values and stays at least distance one from every even function.

items.title: Polynomials vanishing at zero separate points of $[0,1]$ but are not dense in $C([0,1])$
items.strategy: The identity function already separates every pair, so the algebra separates points. Every member and every uniform limit vanishes at zero, so the constant-one function cannot be approximated.

items.title: A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$
Cauchy–Hadamard: the reciprocal radius is $\limsup_{k\to\infty}|a_{k+1}|^{1/(k+1)}$, with the zero and infinite cases included
A real power series converges absolutely inside its radius and diverges outside it, while either behaviour may occur at an endpoint
A power series converges absolutely and uniformly on every closed interval strictly inside its interval of convergence
The sum of a real power series is continuous at every point strictly inside its interval of convergence
A power series, its formal derivative, and its zero-constant-term formal antiderivative have the same radius of convergence
Inside its radius a real power series may be differentiated term by term, and the differentiated series has the same radius
Inside its radius a real power series may be integrated term by term on every closed subinterval
A power-series sum is infinitely differentiable inside its radius and satisfies $a_n=f^{(n)}(c)/\iota(n!)$ at its centre
The binomial double series used to re-expand a power series at an interior point is absolutely convergent and may be regrouped
A power-series sum may be re-expanded about every interior point, with coefficients given by its derivatives there
A real-analytic function on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is locally represented by a convergent real power series
The sum of a real power series is real analytic throughout the open interval determined by its radius
Every real-analytic function is infinitely differentiable
At a zero of a real-analytic function, either some first nonzero coefficient makes the zero isolated or every local coefficient vanishes
Two real-analytic functions on an open interval that agree on a set with an accumulation point in that interval agree throughout the interval
Inside the common radius the product of two power-series sums is represented by the Cauchy product of their coefficients
A composition of convergent real power series has a convergent power-series expansion wherever the inner series maps a neighbourhood into the outer disk of convergence
A convergent real power series with nonzero constant term has a convergent reciprocal power series on a smaller neighbourhood
Real-analytic functions are closed under sums, products and compositions, and under quotients where the denominator is nonzero
Abel summability by $\lim_{x\uparrow1}\sum a_nx^n$ and Cesaro summability by the Cesaro means of the partial sums
Abel's limit theorem: if a real series converges to $s$, then its power series tends to $s$ as $x\uparrow1$
For $0<x<1$, the Abel transform of a series is $(1-x)^2\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)\sigma_nx^n$, where $\sigma_n$ are the Cesaro means of its partial sums
Frobenius' theorem: Cesaro summability of a real series implies Abel summability to the same value
Every convergent real series is Cesaro summable and Abel summable to its ordinary sum
If $\iota(n+1)a_n\to0$, short multiplicative blocks of the coefficients have uniformly small sums
Tauber's theorem: an Abel-summable series with $\iota(n+1)a_n\to0$ converges ordinarily to its Abel sum
FALSE: every power series converges uniformly on its entire open interval of convergence
FALSE: convergence of a power series at one point other than its centre forces convergence at every real point
FALSE: Abel summability alone implies ordinary convergence of a series

pages.title: The Exponential Function

items.title: The real exponential function and the number $e$ by a power series
items.strategy: Define $\exp x=\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ and $e=\exp(1)$. Keep the natural factorial of the finite-counting page distinct from its positive real embedding. The definition is provisional until convergence for every real $x$ is proved in the next item; do not use logarithms or real powers.

items.title: The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument
items.strategy: Fix $x$. Choose a natural $N>2|x|$ by Archimedes. Beyond $N$, consecutive absolute terms shrink by at least $1/2$, so the tail is dominated by a geometric series. Conclude absolute convergence and hence convergence; equivalently the power series has infinite radius. State the factorial recurrence only after embedding it into $\mathbb R$.

items.title: The exponential addition formula $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$
items.strategy: Multiply the two absolutely convergent exponential series using the published Cauchy-product theorem. For coefficient $n$, use the binomial theorem and $\binom{n}{k}/(k!(n-k)!)=1/n!$ after embedding every natural coefficient into $\mathbb R$. This is the only proof of the addition law; do not appeal to an ODE before ODE uniqueness is established.

items.title: The exponential is positive and satisfies $\exp(-x)=1/\exp(x)$
items.strategy: The addition formula gives $\exp(x)\exp(-x)=\exp(0)=1$, so neither factor is zero. Also $\exp(x)=\exp(x/2)^2$ is nonnegative; being nonzero, it is positive. Conclude the reciprocal identity. This proof works for negative $x$ without termwise sign estimates.

items.title: The exponential function is smooth and $(\exp)'=\exp$
items.strategy: Use the infinite radius and the published termwise-differentiation theorem. Shift the derivative series and cancel the embedded factor $\iota(n+1)$ against $\iota((n+1)!)$ to recover the original series. Invoke the power-series smoothness theorem for all higher derivatives.

items.title: The exponential function is strictly increasing
items.strategy: For $x<y$, apply the mean-value theorem to obtain $\exp(y)-\exp(x)=\exp(c)(y-x)$ for some $c\in(x,y)$. Positivity makes the right side strictly positive. Record continuity from the power-series theorem and do not infer strict increase merely from a nonnegative derivative.

items.title: The exponential tends to $+\infty$ at $+\infty$ and to $0$ at $-\infty$
items.strategy: For $x\ge0$, the first two series terms give $\exp x\ge1+x$, hence divergence to $+\infty$. Use $\exp(-x)=1/\exp x$ for the negative limit. Conclude that the range is contained in the positive reals and approaches both endpoints of that interval. Use the definitions of limits at infinity rather than informal asymptotics.

items.title: The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb R$ onto $(0,\infty)$
items.strategy: Strict increase gives injectivity. Given $y>0$, the two endpoint limits give $a<b$ with $\exp(a)<y<\exp(b)$, and the intermediate-value theorem gives a preimage. Positivity excludes every nonpositive value. Do not name the inverse logarithm on this page.

items.title: The exponential dominates every fixed nonnegative integer power at $+\infty$
items.strategy: For $m\in\mathbb N$, $a>0$ and $x>0$, retain the $(m+1)$-st nonnegative term of the series for $\exp(ax)$ to get $\exp(ax)\ge (ax)^{m+1}/\iota((m+1)!)$. Hence $0\le x^m/\exp(ax)\le\iota((m+1)!)/(a^{m+1}x)\to0$. State only domination of fixed nonnegative integer powers.

items.title: The exponential is the unique solution of $y'=y$ with $y(0)=1$
items.strategy: Existence is the derivative theorem and $\exp(0)=1$. For uniqueness, if $y'=y$, differentiate $y(x)\exp(-x)$ using product and chain rules; its derivative is zero, so the product is constant and equals $1$. Positivity permits division. Include the interval-local version with an arbitrary initial value $y(a)=c$, yielding $y(x)=c\exp(x-a)$.

items.title: Regular normalized multiplicative Cauchy equations characterize the exponential
items.strategy: Prove two clauses. First, if $F(x+y)=F(x)F(y)$ and $F$ is differentiable at $0$ with $F(0)=1$ and $F'(0)=1$, then a translated difference quotient gives $F'=F$, so IVP uniqueness gives $F=\exp$. Second, if $F$ is continuous, multiplicative, and $F(1)=e$, then $F>0$, agrees with $\exp$ on rationals by uniqueness of positive roots, and agrees everywhere by density and continuity. Treat the identically-zero multiplicative solution separately before asserting $F(0)=1$.

items.title: For fixed $k$, $\binom{n}{k}/n^k$ tends to $1/k!$
items.strategy: For $n\ge k$, use the proved closed formula to write $\iota\binom{n}{k}/\iota(n)^k=(1/\iota(k!))\prod_{j<k}(1-\iota(j)/\iota(n))$. Each factor lies in $[0,1]$ and tends to $1$, so the product tends to $1$ and the coefficient is uniformly between $0$ and $1/\iota(k!)$. Include $k=0$ and state the natural-to-real embeddings at every division.

items.title: For every real $x$, $(1+x/n)^n\to\exp x$
items.strategy: Take $n>|x|$ so the base is positive and expand by the binomial theorem. For a fixed finite head, the scaled-binomial lemma gives convergence to the corresponding exponential terms. Bound the remaining binomial tail uniformly by the tail of $\sum |x|^k/k!$, then choose the head by convergence of that series. This finite-head/infinite-tail proof works for negative $x$ and contains no logarithm.

items.title: Picard iteration from $1$ produces the exponential partial sums
items.strategy: Define $P_0(x)=1$ and $P_{n+1}(x)=1+\int_0^xP_n(t)\,dt$. Inductively use the power rule and the working FTC to prove $P_n(x)=\sum_{k\le n}x^k/\iota(k!)$. Uniform convergence on compact intervals gives $P_n\to\exp$, and the uniform-limit integration theorem yields $\exp(x)=1+\int_0^x\exp(t)dt$. Conversely differentiate that integral equation to recover the IVP.

items.title: The power-series, product-limit, IVP, functional-equation, and Picard definitions agree
items.strategy: Collect the preceding results as an equivalence theorem: E1 is the defining series; E2 is the product limit; E3 is the normalized IVP; E6 is either regular normalized multiplicative Cauchy condition; and E11 is the Picard integral iteration. For each arrow cite the theorem that already proves it rather than repeating proofs. State the normalization in every formulation so no one-parameter family is accidentally identified with $\exp$.

items.title: A geometric bound for tails of the exponential series
items.strategy: For real $x$ and $N$ with $\iota(N+2)\ge2|x|$, consecutive absolute terms after index $N+1$ have ratio at most $1/2$. Compare the tail with the geometric series of ratio $1/2$ to obtain $\sum_{k=N+1}^{\infty}|x|^k/\iota(k!)\le2|x|^{N+1}/\iota((N+1)!)$.

items.title: The elementary numerical bound $2<e<3$
items.strategy: The first two terms and the positive remaining tail give $e>2$. For the upper bound apply the factorial-tail estimate at $n=1$ carefully (or sum the sharper geometric comparison beginning with $1/2!$) to obtain a strict bound below $3$. Avoid decimal approximations.

items.title: The number $e$ is irrational
items.strategy: Assume $e=p/q$ with integers $p$ and positive $q$. Choose a natural $n>q$. Then $\iota(n!)e$ and $\iota(n!)\sum_{k\le n}1/k!$ are integers, so their positive difference is an integer. The factorial-tail bound makes it strictly between $0$ and $1$, a contradiction. Prove the divisibility/cancellation step with the factorial definition and identify integer and real embeddings explicitly.

items.title: The exponential roadmap and its circularity hazards
items.strategy: Record the five equivalent constructions proved here and the proof order: series before addition, addition before positivity, derivative before IVP uniqueness, and all of these before characterization. State that logarithms and arbitrary real powers are deferred. Distinguish the published rational-power operation from $\exp(x\log a)$, which is unavailable. Record that the compact bump is in the companion page but a general smooth partition of unity and a nowhere-analytic smooth function are outside this dependency-closed scope.

items.title: The log-free product limit $(1-2/n)^n\to\exp(-2)$
items.strategy: Apply the product-limit theorem at $x=-2$, noting that the base is positive for $n>2$. Expand several finite cases only as a sanity check; the proof uses the general finite-head/tail theorem, not a nonexistent logarithm of a negative or zero base.

items.title: The convergence $(1+x/n)^n\to\exp x$ is not uniform on $\mathbb R$
items.strategy: For each $n$, evaluate at $x=n$. The approximant is $2^n$, whereas $\exp(n)=e^n$ by repeated use of the addition formula. Since $e>2$, the difference is at least $e^n-2^n$ and does not tend to zero. State uniform convergence using the published definition and note that the base is positive at these witnesses.

items.title: The one-sided flat function is $C^\infty$ with identically zero Taylor series
items.strategy: Define $\phi(x)=\exp(-1/x^2)$ for $x>0$ and $\phi(x)=0$ for $x\le0$. Inductively show on $x>0$ that $\phi^{(n)}(x)=P_n(1/x)\exp(-1/x^2)$ for a polynomial $P_n$. Exponential domination makes every one-sided derivative limit at $0$ equal $0$, so all derivatives glue and vanish there. The function is positive for $x>0$, hence differs from its zero Maclaurin series in every right neighbourhood.

items.title: A nonzero smooth compactly supported bump
items.strategy: Define $\psi(x)=\exp(-1/(1-x^2))$ for $|x|<1$ and $0$ for $|x|\ge1$. On the open interval smoothness follows from the chain and algebra rules. At $\pm1$, reduce each one-sided derivative to the flat-function estimate after factoring $1-x^2$ and prove all derivatives tend to $0$. Conclude $\psi\in C^\infty$, is positive on $(-1,1)$, and has support $[-1,1]$. Do not claim a general partition of unity.

items.title: A discontinuous positive solution of $F(x+y)=F(x)F(y)$
items.strategy: Assuming the Axiom of Choice, extend the $\mathbb Q$-independent set $\{1,\alpha\}$ to a Hamel basis of $\mathbb R$ over $\mathbb Q$. Define an additive non-linear $h$ by assigning incompatible basis values, and put $F=\exp\circ h$. The addition formula makes $F$ positive and multiplicative. If $F$ were continuous, strict injectivity of $\exp$ would force enough regularity on $h$ to contradict its construction; alternatively use the normalized functional-equation theorem after rescaling. State the choice cost explicitly.

items.title: The exponential is not uniformly continuous on $\mathbb R$
items.strategy: Take $x_n=n$ and $y_n=n+1/n$. Their distance tends to $0$, but the MVT gives $\exp(y_n)-\exp(x_n)=\exp(c_n)/n\ge e^n/n$, which is bounded away from $0$ and in fact diverges. Justify the last growth from exponential domination. Contrast with Heine–Cantor on every compact interval.

items.title: Intervals in a poset; locally finite, lower-finite and upper-finite posets
items.strategy: Define $[x,y]=\{z:x\le z\le y\}$. Locally finite means every such interval is finite; lower-finite and upper-finite mean every principal ideal and principal filter is finite. State that either one-sided condition implies local finiteness.

items.title: A finite sum in a commutative monoid indexed by an arbitrary finite set
items.strategy: Enumerate the finite index set, use the monoid finite-product construction in additive notation, and prove independence of the enumeration from generalised commutativity. Record agreement with the published real- and natural-valued finite-index-set sum.

items.title: Finite commutative-monoid sums are invariant under bijective reindexing, split over disjoint unions, and satisfy the finite Fubini rule
items.strategy: Reduce reindexing to permutation invariance, disjoint unions to concatenated enumerations, and the double sum to an enumeration of the finite Cartesian product.

items.title: The incidence functions $I(P,R)$ of a locally finite poset and their convolution
items.strategy: For a locally finite poset $P$ and commutative ring $R$, define functions on comparable pairs and $(f*g)(x,y)=\sum_{x\le z\le y}f(x,z)g(z,y)$. Local finiteness and the general finite-sum definition make the operation well defined.

items.title: The delta and zeta incidence functions
items.strategy: Define $\delta(x,y)=1$ when $x=y$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\zeta(x,y)=1$ on every comparable pair.

items.title: Incidence convolution is associative and distributes over pointwise addition
items.strategy: Expand both bracketings as the same finite sum over pairs $x\le u\le v\le y$, using finite Fubini and bijective reindexing. Prove both distributive laws termwise.

items.title: Pointwise addition and convolution make $I(P,R)$ a ring with identity $\delta$
items.strategy: Obtain the pointwise additive abelian group from the function-ring construction, use the preceding lemma for multiplication and distributivity, and compute $\delta*f=f=f*\delta$.

items.title: If every diagonal value of an incidence function is a unit, recursive interval formulas construct both a left and a right convolution inverse
items.strategy: Use strong induction on the finite cardinality of $[x,y]$. Solve the equations $(f*g)(x,y)=0$ and $(h*f)(x,y)=0$ off the diagonal after isolating the diagonal unit. Then $h=h*(f*g)=(h*f)*g=g$, so the one-sided inverses coincide.

items.title: An incidence function is convolution-invertible if and only if every diagonal value is a unit
items.strategy: Necessity follows by evaluating an inverse equation on $(x,x)$. Sufficiency is the recursive construction. State the criterion for arbitrary locally finite $P$, including infinite $P$.

items.title: The integer-valued Möbius function $\mu_P$ of a locally finite poset
items.strategy: Take the inverse of the zeta function in $I(P,\mathbb Z)$. Existence and uniqueness come from the invertibility criterion because every diagonal value is $1$. This fixes the coefficient ring as $\mathbb Z$ and avoids a characteristic-dependent second notion.

items.title: The Möbius recurrence: $\mu_P(x,x)=1$ and both interval sums of $\mu_P$ vanish when $x<y$
items.strategy: Evaluate $\mu*\zeta=\delta$ and $\zeta*\mu=\delta$. Isolate the endpoint term to obtain the two recursive formulas and uniqueness.

items.title: Möbius inversion on a lower-finite poset, with the dual upper-finite form
items.strategy: For functions $f,g:P\to R$ into a commutative ring, prove $g(y)=\sum_{x\le y}f(x)$ iff $f(y)=\sum_{x\le y}\mu_P(x,y)g(x)$. Interchange the finite double sum and use the recurrence. State and prove the order-dual upper-finite form separately.

items.title: Both forms of Möbius inversion hold on every finite poset
items.strategy: Every principal ideal and filter is a subset of the finite ground set, hence finite; apply both halves of the preceding theorem.

items.title: The Möbius function of a product poset is the product of the Möbius functions
items.strategy: Show intervals in $P\times Q$ are Cartesian products of intervals and hence finite. Verify that the proposed product satisfies the Möbius recurrence using finite Fubini.

items.title: For $A\subseteq B$ in a finite Boolean lattice, $\mu(A,B)=(-1)^{\lvert B\setminus A\rvert}$
items.strategy: Identify the interval $[A,B]$ with a product of two-element chains indexed by $B\setminus A$, then apply the product theorem. Alternatively verify the recurrence by the alternating binomial sum; keep one route as the proof and the other as a Remark.

items.title: The complementary inclusion-exclusion formula is Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice
items.strategy: Index intersections by subsets of the sieve index set, apply finite-poset Möbius inversion, insert the Boolean-lattice formula, and match every term and sign to the published complementary sieve identity.

items.title: On a finite chain, the Möbius function is $1$ on the diagonal, $-1$ on covers and $0$ on longer intervals
items.strategy: Induct on interval cardinality using the recurrence. The first nontrivial interval gives $-1$ and every longer interval has partial sum $1-1=0$ before the final term.

items.title: The divisibility poset of positive integers
items.strategy: Restrict integer divisibility to positive integers and verify reflexivity, antisymmetry and transitivity. Its interval $[a,b]$ consists of the positive integers $d$ with $a\mid d\mid b$.

items.title: The divisibility poset is lower-finite, and each divisor interval factorises as a product of finite chains of prime exponents
items.strategy: Positive divisors of $n$ lie in a finite initial segment. Use canonical prime factorisation and valuations to biject divisors with exponent tuples $0\le e_i\le v_{p_i}(n)$, preserving and reflecting divisibility.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function $\mu(n)$ from prime factorisation
items.strategy: For $n\ge1$, set $\mu(n)=0$ when some prime square divides $n$, and $\mu(n)=(-1)^r$ when $n$ is a product of $r$ distinct primes. Use uniqueness of prime factorisation to prove $r$ and the value are well defined, including $\mu(1)=1$.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function is the poset Möbius function of divisibility: $\mu(n)=\mu_{\mid}(1,n)$
items.strategy: Use the prime-exponent product decomposition of the divisor interval, the product theorem and the finite-chain formula. A repeated prime exponent contributes zero; otherwise every nontrivial chain contributes $-1$.

items.title: Classical Möbius inversion over positive divisors
items.strategy: Apply lower-finite poset inversion to the divisibility order and substitute the agreement theorem. Give both standard equivalent indexings, with $\mu(d)$ and with $\mu(n/d)$.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function is multiplicative on coprime positive integers
items.strategy: For coprime $m,n$, divisors of $mn$ split uniquely into a divisor of $m$ and a divisor of $n$ by prime factorisation. Apply the product-poset theorem and the agreement theorem.

items.title: False: convolution defines an incidence algebra for every poset
items.strategy: Refute with the companion's poset having an infinite interval: convolution of the constant-one functions asks for an infinite sum not defined by the ring axioms.

items.title: False: $\mu_P(x,y)$ depends only on the cardinality of $[x,y]$
items.strategy: Compare a four-element chain, whose endpoint value is $0$, with the four-element diamond, whose endpoint value is $1$.

items.title: False: classical Möbius inversion and inclusion-exclusion are unrelated inversion principles
items.strategy: Refute by citing their common finite-poset inversion theorem and the two dictionary results for the divisibility and Boolean posets.

items.title: The full Möbius table of the Boolean lattice $2^{[3]}$
items.strategy: List comparable pairs by rank difference and assign $1,-1,1,-1$ according to the Boolean-lattice formula, checking representative recurrence sums.

items.title: The Möbius table of a four-element chain
items.strategy: Compute recursively: diagonal entries are $1$, cover entries are $-1$, and all entries spanning at least two covers are $0$.

items.title: The Möbius function on the divisor poset of $12$ and its agreement with $\mu(1),\mu(2),\mu(3),\mu(4),\mu(6),\mu(12)$
items.strategy: Draw the divisor order, compute from the recurrence, and compare each value with the prime-factor definition.

items.title: The endpoint Möbius value of the four-element diamond is $1$
items.strategy: Compute the two cover values as $-1$, then solve $1-1-1+\mu(\bot,\top)=0$.

items.title: Möbius inversion of $\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n$ gives $\varphi(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)(n/d)$
items.strategy: Apply classical Möbius inversion to the totient divisor-sum theorem and verify the formula numerically at $n=12$.

items.title: A poset with a bottom, a top and countably many incomparable middle elements has an infinite interval, so convolution of constant-one functions is not defined
items.strategy: Use the tagged set $\{\bot,\top\}\cup(\mathbb N\times\{m\})$, with every middle element strictly between the endpoints. The endpoint convolution sum has one term for each middle element.

items.title: On a two-element chain, an incidence function with a zero diagonal value is not convolution-invertible
items.strategy: Set $f(0,0)=0$ and evaluate any purported inverse equation on $(0,0)$; the diagonal product remains zero rather than one.

items.title: A four-element chain and a four-element diamond have equal-size endpoint intervals but Möbius values $0$ and $1$
items.strategy: Place the two preceding computations side by side and identify the different internal order structures that change the recurrence.

items.title: Total differentiability gives a local $O(\|h\|_2)$ increment bound and therefore continuity
items.strategy: Bound $Df(a)h$ by the Euclidean linear-map lemma and make the normalized remainder at most one on a sufficiently small ball. The triangle inequality gives $\|f(a+h)-f(a)\|_2\le(K+1)\|h\|_2$, from which epsilon-delta continuity follows; keep the zero-map and zero-increment cases explicit.

items.title: The Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives and the gradient in the scalar-valued case
A total derivative computes every directional derivative, and its matrix is the Jacobian
items.strategy: Restrict the total remainder estimate to $h=tv$. After division by $t$, homogeneity makes the remainder tend to zero and the derivative of $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ equals $Df(a)v$. Specialize to standard basis vectors and invoke the matrix-column representation to identify the Jacobian, preserving the $v=0$ case.

items.title: For a differentiable scalar field, $D_vf(a)=\langle\nabla f(a),v\rangle$ and the unit direction of steepest ascent is the normalized gradient
items.strategy: Use the Jacobian representation in the scalar case to obtain the inner-product formula. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds unit-direction derivatives by the gradient norm, with equality in the normalized gradient direction when the gradient is nonzero; when it is zero, every directional derivative is zero and there is no unique steepest direction.

items.title: Sums and scalar multiples of totally differentiable maps are totally differentiable with the expected derivatives
items.strategy: Add or scale the two remainder identities and use the norm triangle inequality or absolute homogeneity. Verify that the proposed derivative is linear, and split the scalar-zero case only where division by its absolute value would otherwise occur.

items.title: The chain rule for total derivatives: $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$
items.strategy: Write $f(a+h)-f(a)=Ah+r(h)$ and $g(f(a)+k)-g(f(a))=Bk+s(k)$. The local linear bound makes $k=O(\|h\|)$, so $s(k)=o(\|k\|)=o(\|h\|)$, while boundedness of $B$ gives $B r(h)=o(\|h\|)$. Treat $k=0$ without forming the normalized outer remainder and verify the composite linear map explicitly.

items.title: Small coordinate-by-coordinate increments stay inside a Euclidean ball and telescope the total increment
items.strategy: For $h\in\mathbb{R}^m$, define $p_j=a+\sum_{k<j}h_ke_k$. The norm of each coordinate prefix is at most $\|h\|_2$, so a small increment keeps every $p_j$ in the chosen ball. The finite telescoping identity expresses $f(a+h)-f(a)$ as the sum of the increments $f(p_{j+1})-f(p_j)$.

items.title: If all partial derivatives exist on a neighbourhood and are continuous at a point, then the map is totally differentiable there with Jacobian derivative
items.strategy: Choose a ball where every partial derivative vector is uniformly close to its value at the base point. Telescope along coordinate segments using the preceding lemma; apply the published vector mean-value inequality to each segment after subtracting the fixed linear term. Sum the errors and compare the coordinate $1$-norm with the Euclidean norm. Verify the Jacobian map is linear before invoking the definition.

items.title: On a convex open set, a uniform bound $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ implies $\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2$
items.strategy: Parametrize the segment from $x$ to $y$ by $\gamma(t)=x+t(y-x)$. Convexity keeps the curve in the domain, the chain rule gives $(f\circ\gamma)'(t)=Df(\gamma(t))(y-x)$, and the published vector mean-value inequality supplies the endpoint estimate. Treat $x=y$ directly and use no global operator-norm definition.

items.title: A totally differentiable map with zero derivative on a convex open set is constant
items.strategy: Apply the total-derivative mean-value inequality with $M=0$ to arbitrary points of the domain. Include the empty-domain case (vacuously constant under the library's definition) and singleton/zero-dimensional exclusions explicitly rather than importing the later connected-open-set theorem.

items.title: Dimension, openness, norm, Jacobian, and the native Euclidean linear-map agreement seam

pages.title: The Total Derivative in R^m -> R^n: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The polynomial map $(x,y)\mapsto(1+x+2y+x^2,\,2x+3y+xy)$ and its Jacobian
items.strategy: Compute all four partial derivatives with the one-variable algebra and power rules. Their continuity makes the continuous-partials theorem applicable, and the resulting Jacobian matrix gives the total derivative at an arbitrary point. Verify one increment expansion directly as a check on the matrix.

items.title: $xy/(x^2+y^2)$ has both partial derivatives at the origin but is discontinuous there
items.strategy: Define the value at the origin to be zero. Both coordinate-axis restrictions are identically zero, so both partial derivatives exist and vanish. Along $y=x\ne0$ the function is $1/2$, contradicting continuity at the origin.

items.title: $x^2y/(x^4+y^2)$ tends to zero on every line through the origin but not along $y=x^2$
items.strategy: Define the origin value to be zero. Substitute $(x,y)=(ta,tb)$ and separate $b=0$ from $b\ne0$ to show every straight-line restriction tends to zero. Along $(t,t^2)$ the value is $1/2$, so the map is not continuous at the origin.

items.title: $x^2y/(x^2+y^2)$ has every directional derivative at the origin but is not totally differentiable there
items.strategy: Compute the directional derivative along $v=(a,b)$ as $a^2b/(a^2+b^2)$ for $v\ne0$ and zero for $v=0$. Exhibit a failure of additivity of this direction map. If a total derivative existed, the directional-derivative theorem would make the map linear, a contradiction.

items.title: The map $y(x^2+y^2)/x$ off the line $x=0$, extended by zero on that line, has every directional derivative zero at the origin but is discontinuous there
items.strategy: On every fixed line through the origin the function is quadratic in the line parameter, so the directional difference quotient tends to zero. Along the curved path $x=y^3$ the values tend to one, proving discontinuity and hence failure of total differentiability.

items.title: A locally constant step map on the disconnected open set $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ has zero total derivative but is not globally Lipschitz
items.strategy: In the $\mathbb{R}^1$ identification, take value zero on the negative component and one on the positive component. Each point has a neighbourhood on which the map is constant, so its total derivative is zero. The points $-t$ and $t$ have image distance one and domain distance $2t$, which defeats every proposed global Lipschitz constant for small positive $t$.

pages.title: Mixed Partials, Taylor, and Extrema in Several Variables

items.title: $C^k$ maps and multi-index derivative notation in Euclidean space
The Hessian matrix and critical points of a scalar field
A rectangular second difference equals a mixed partial times the side lengths
items.strategy: Apply the one-variable mean value theorem in one coordinate to the difference across the other coordinate, then apply it again to the resulting one-variable function. State the closed-rectangle and interior differentiability hypotheses exactly.

items.title: Peano's mixed-partial theorem from continuity of one mixed partial
items.strategy: Apply the rectangle formula to shrinking rectangles based at the point. Continuity of one mixed partial controls the quotient, while the assumed existence of the reverse iterated derivative along the coordinate line identifies the other iterated limit.

items.title: Young's theorem: total differentiability of the first partials forces equality of mixed partials
items.strategy: Expand the two first-partial functions at the base point with total-derivative remainders and insert those expansions into a symmetric rectangular difference quotient. Cancellation leaves the two mixed coefficients equal.

items.title: Clairaut–Schwarz theorem for continuous second partial derivatives
items.strategy: Continuity of the relevant second partials gives the hypotheses of Peano's theorem (and, alternatively, Young's differentiability hypothesis); specialize to every coordinate pair.

items.title: The Hessian of a $C^2$ scalar field is symmetric
items.strategy: Apply Clairaut–Schwarz to each pair of coordinate indices and translate the equalities into matrix entries.

items.title: Continuous mixed partials of order $k$ are invariant under permutations
items.strategy: Show invariance under one adjacent transposition by applying Clairaut–Schwarz after freezing the other derivatives; decompose every finite permutation into adjacent transpositions and induct over their number.

items.title: Repeated derivatives along a line expand by the multinomial formula
items.strategy: Apply the total-derivative chain rule once, then induct on the derivative order. Use symmetry of higher mixed partials to collect ordered coordinate choices into multinomial coefficients.

items.title: The multivariable Taylor polynomial in multi-index notation
Multivariable Taylor formula with a Lagrange remainder along a line segment
items.strategy: Restrict the function to the segment, apply the one-variable Lagrange Taylor formula, and substitute the line-derivative multinomial expansion. Convexity keeps the segment inside the domain; separate zero increment.

items.title: Multivariable Taylor formula with $o(\|h\|^k)$ remainder
items.strategy: Apply the one-variable Peano theorem to the line restriction and use the multinomial line-derivative identity; convert the scalar parameter remainder to the Euclidean increment norm.

items.title: Second-order Taylor expansion $f(a+h)=f(a)+\nabla f(a)\cdot h+\tfrac12h^TH_f(a)h+o(\|h\|^2)$
items.strategy: Specialize the Peano formula to order two and collect the first- and second-order multi-index terms as the gradient inner product and Hessian quadratic form.

items.title: Local and strict local extrema for scalar fields on Euclidean open sets
Fermat's theorem: an interior differentiable local extremum has zero gradient
items.strategy: Restrict to each coordinate line through the point, apply the one-variable Fermat theorem, and identify the resulting partial derivatives as the gradient coordinates.

items.title: Positive definite, negative definite, semidefinite, and indefinite quadratic forms
A definite quadratic form has a uniform signed bound on the Euclidean unit sphere
items.strategy: For $n\ge 1$, prove directly that the Euclidean unit sphere is nonempty, closed, and bounded: use $e_0$ for nonemptiness, continuity of the Euclidean norm for closedness, and the norm equation for boundedness. Heine-Borel then makes the sphere compact. Prove continuity of the fixed quadratic form from its finite coordinate formula, apply the extreme value theorem, and use definiteness to make the attained minimum positive or the attained maximum negative.

items.title: The multivariable second-derivative test by definiteness of the Hessian
items.strategy: At a critical point combine the second-order Taylor expansion with the uniform sphere bound. Positive or negative definiteness dominates the little-o remainder and gives a strict extremum; two directions of opposite quadratic sign give saddle behaviour. Make the semidefinite case explicitly inconclusive.

items.title: The two-variable Hessian determinant test
items.strategy: For the symmetric matrix with entries $A,B,C$, complete the square when $A\ne0$. The determinant sign classifies definiteness or indefiniteness; if the determinant is zero, state that the test gives no conclusion.

items.title: A constrained local extremum annihilates every velocity of a differentiable parametrization
items.strategy: Compose the objective with each differentiable curve in the constraint set through the point. One-variable Fermat and the total-derivative chain rule give $Df(a)\gamma'(0)=0$.

items.title: Lagrange multipliers for a regular graph constraint $y=\psi(x)$
items.strategy: Parametrize the graph by $x\mapsto(x,\psi(x))$. The parametrized necessary condition says the objective gradient is orthogonal to all graph tangent vectors; solve the coordinate equations to obtain $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla(y-\psi(x))$, whose last coordinate is nonzero.

pages.title: Mixed Partials, Taylor, and Extrema in Several Variables: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Peano's function has unequal mixed partials at the origin
items.strategy: For $f(x,y)=xy(x^2-y^2)/(x^2+y^2)$ off the origin and zero at the origin, compute the two axis first partials and then their derivatives at zero, obtaining opposite values. Also verify continuity at the origin by a quadratic bound.

items.title: Peano's surface has a strict minimum on every line through the origin but no local extremum
items.strategy: Use $f(x,y)=(y-3x^2)(y-x^2)$. Substitution on an arbitrary line gives a positive leading even power near zero, with vertical lines separate; along the parabola $y=2x^2$ the values are negative.

items.title: A smooth flat refinement has a strict minimum on every line through the origin but no local extremum
items.strategy: Let $\phi(x)=e^{-1/x^2}$ for $x\ne0$ and $\phi(0)=0$, and set $F=(y-3\phi(x))(y-\phi(x))$. Exponential domination proves smooth flatness and linewise positivity; the curve $y=2\phi(x)$ gives negative values approaching the origin.

items.title: $x^2+y^2(1-x)^3$ has a unique critical point, a strict local but nonglobal minimum
items.strategy: Solve the two gradient equations to show the origin is the sole critical point. Its Hessian is positive definite, while values with $x>1$ and sufficiently large $|y|$ are negative, so the local minimum is not global.

items.title: The monkey saddle $x^3-3xy^2$ has an indefinite higher-order critical point
items.strategy: Compute the zero gradient and zero Hessian at the origin, then evaluate along three rays to exhibit alternating signs. Conclude directly that the origin is a saddle although the quadratic test is silent.

items.title: A zero Hessian occurs at a strict minimum, a strict maximum, and a saddle
items.strategy: Compare $x^4+y^4$, $-(x^4+y^4)$, and $x^4-y^4$ at the origin. Compute the common zero gradient and Hessian, then classify by signs.

items.title: A second-order Taylor polynomial computed from gradient and Hessian data
items.strategy: For $f(x,y)=e^x(1+y+y^2)$ at the origin, compute the value, gradient, and Hessian and substitute them into the second-order formula; verify the coefficients by multiplying the one-variable expansions.

items.title: A constrained extremum on an affine graph satisfies the graph Lagrange rule
items.strategy: Minimize $x^2+y^2$ on $y=x+1$ by completing the square in the graph parameter, then compute both gradients and the multiplier at the unique minimizer.

items.title: The degenerate constraint $x^2+y^2=0$ defeats the multiplier conclusion
items.strategy: The constraint set is the singleton origin, so $f(x,y)=x$ has a constrained extremum there. But $\nabla g(0,0)=0$ and $\nabla f(0,0)=(1,0)$, so no scalar multiplier can satisfy the usual equation.
