pages.title: The Riemann Integral in R^m and Jordan Content

items.title: Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb R^m$ and their volume
items.strategy: Fix $m\geq1$. For vectors $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\leq b_j$, define $[a,b]=\{x:a_j\leq x_j\leq b_j\text{ for }j<m\}$ and $\operatorname{vol}([a,b])=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j)$. Call the rectangle nondegenerate when every inequality is strict. The finite product is the published recursive product, so volume exists; prove nonnegativity and the effect of a coordinate cut. State that at $m=1$ this is the published interval and its length.

items.title: Grid partitions of a rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$, their cells, refinements and mesh
items.strategy: A grid partition is a list of one-dimensional partitions indexed by $j<m$. Its cells are indexed by the multi-indices $i\in\mathbb N^m$ satisfying $i_j<n_j$, and each cell is the product of the corresponding subintervals. Define every sum over cells as an iterated finite sum, recursively in the $m$ coordinate index ranges; this avoids importing the finite-index-set sum from a page outside the fixed prerequisite closure. Define the mesh as the maximum coordinate subinterval length; by the norm/metric dictionary this is the $d_\infty$ diameter of the largest cell. Define coordinatewise refinement and common refinement, prove the cells cover the rectangle with disjoint interiors, and prove by induction on $m$ that the iterated sum of cell volumes is the rectangle volume. No multidimensional partition or sum may be left as an informal picture.

items.title: Lower and upper Darboux sums over a grid partition in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: For bounded $f$ on a nondegenerate rectangle and each grid cell $Q_i$, take $m_i=\inf f[Q_i]$ and $M_i=\sup f[Q_i]$, then form the iterated finite sums of $m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)$ and $M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)$ fixed in the grid definition. Prove the extrema exist, the sums are finite reals, and lower sum $\leq$ upper sum. Record that the gap is the corresponding iterated sum of cell oscillations times cell volumes.

items.title: Refinement raises multidimensional lower sums and lowers upper sums, with a quantitative boundary-slab estimate
items.strategy: For one inserted coordinate hyperplane, split the relevant coordinate sum and group the resulting iterated finite sums inside each old cell to prove monotonicity. Iterate coordinatewise for a general refinement. Add the quantitative clause needed for mesh-based Riemann sums: after refining an arbitrary fine grid by one fixed grid, only cells meeting the fixed interior hyperplanes can change the coarse Darboux bounds; their total volume is bounded by a fixed cross-sectional constant times the fine mesh. Prove that slab bound by induction and finite-product distributivity rather than appealing to measure or to sums over abstract finite sets.

items.title: The lower and upper Darboux integrals over a nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: On a nondegenerate rectangle, take the supremum of all lower grid sums and infimum of all upper grid sums, and call $f$ integrable when they agree. The endpoint grids are nonempty, refinement bounds the two sum families, and completeness plus the infimum theorem supplies the extrema. Do not define an integral on degenerate rectangles, because the grid definition requires strict coordinate partitions.

items.title: Riemann's criterion on a nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$: integrability is equivalent to arbitrarily small Darboux gaps
items.strategy: On a nondegenerate rectangle, repeat the published supremum/infimum argument with grid partitions: equality of the lower and upper integrals gives grids good for the two sides and their common refinement is good for both. Conversely one small Darboux gap bounds the integral gap.

items.title: Tagged grid partitions and Riemann sums in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: A tagging assigns one point to each multi-indexed grid cell. A canonical lower-corner tagging proves existence without choice; when arbitrary cellwise selections are needed, enumerate the finitely nested coordinate ranges and apply finite choice inductively. Define $S(f,P,\xi)$ by the iterated finite-sum convention of the grid definition. Define mesh convergence to $I$ by requiring every tagged grid of sufficiently small mesh to have sum near $I$. Prove each Riemann sum lies between the Darboux sums of the same grid.

items.title: The multidimensional Darboux and tagged-mesh definitions of the Riemann integral agree
items.strategy: The easy direction traps every tagged sum between the Darboux sums of one grid. For the converse, choose a fixed grid with small Darboux gap, refine an arbitrary sufficiently fine grid by it, and use the quantitative boundary-slab estimate to control the change in upper and lower sums. Choose near-extremal tags cellwise by finite choice, exactly as the published one-dimensional proof does. This is a long proof already decomposed by the refinement lemma; do not rebuild that estimate inside the theorem.

items.title: At $m=1$, nondegenerate multidimensional rectangles, grid sums and the integral are exactly the published one-dimensional notions
items.strategy: Identify $\mathbb R^1$ with $\mathbb R$. Nondegeneracy is exactly $a<b$; a coordinate grid is one ordinary partition, its cells are the published subintervals, volume is length, and both Darboux and tagged sums agree term for term. Conclude that the integrability classes and values coincide.

items.title: Linearity, monotonicity, the absolute-value estimate and coordinate-slice additivity for the Riemann integral in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: On a nondegenerate rectangle prove linearity and monotonicity from Darboux gaps and identify values through tagged-sum convergence; derive $|\int f|\le\int|f|$. For a strictly interior coordinate cut, splice coordinate partitions and split the nested finite sum to obtain additivity and the converse integrability statement. Endpoint cuts are excluded because they create degenerate subrectangles, for which this integral is not defined.

items.title: Every continuous function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable
items.strategy: A closed nondegenerate rectangle is compact by Heine-Borel. Metric Heine-Cantor makes a continuous scalar function uniformly continuous, and the extreme-value theorem makes it bounded. A grid below the uniform-continuity threshold has small oscillation on every cell, so the multidimensional Riemann criterion applies.

items.title: Measure zero and content zero in $\mathbb R^m$ by countable and finite cube covers
items.strategy: For $m\geq1$, define a closed axis-parallel cube and its volume. A set is null when for every $\varepsilon>0$ it has a countable cube cover whose volume series is at most $\varepsilon$; it has content zero when a finite such cover exists. Cube covers are chosen because Lipschitz images are controlled by cubes without aspect-ratio defects. Prove inheritance by subsets and finite-cover padding. Do not define Lebesgue measure or outer measure.

items.title: At $m=1$, cube-nullity and cube-content-zero are exactly the published interval-cover notions
items.strategy: Under the isometry $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$, a closed cube is a closed interval and its volume is its length. The countable and finite cover quantifiers, including their finite-sum and series bounds, are therefore word for word those of the published definition. Record both directions explicitly so later items may move between the vocabularies.

items.title: Subsets and countable unions of null subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ are null
items.strategy: Subset closure is immediate. For a sequence of null sets, assign the $j$-th set a geometric fraction of the $\varepsilon$ budget, use countable choice to select one cube cover for each set, and enumerate the doubly indexed cubes through the published bijection $\mathbb N^2\to\mathbb N$. Bound finite partial sums by finite rectangles of indices, as the published one-dimensional theorem does. State the countable-choice cost in the theorem.

items.title: For compact subsets of $\mathbb R^m$, measure zero and content zero coincide
items.strategy: Content zero implies nullity by padding. Conversely enlarge every closed covering cube slightly to an open cube, spending a geometric fraction of the remaining volume budget; compactness gives a finite subcover, and bounding its finitely many indices controls the total enlarged volume. Use Heine–Borel only to identify compact sets when needed, not as a substitute for the finite-subcover definition.

items.title: Oscillation of a real function on subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ and at a point
items.strategy: For $f:A\to\mathbb R$ define $\omega_f(S)=\sup\{|f(x)-f(y)|:x,y\in S\}$ in the extended reals and $\omega_f(c)=\inf_{r>0}\omega_f(A\cap B(c,r))$, using Euclidean balls. Prove well-posedness and monotonicity under inclusion as in the published real-domain definition. Include the dictionary clause that under $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ this is exactly `def-oscillation`.

items.title: A function on a subset of $\mathbb R^m$ is continuous at $x$ iff its oscillation there is $0$, and every oscillation superlevel set is closed
items.strategy: Translate the epsilon definition of metric continuity into small oscillation on a ball for one direction; for the other, use one point fixed at $x$ in the oscillation bound. To prove $\{x:\omega_f(x)\geq\varepsilon\}$ closed relative to the domain, show its complement is open: one ball with oscillation below $\varepsilon$ works for every sufficiently nearby centre after shrinking the radius. State the result for bounded $f$ when real-valued oscillations are needed by integration.

items.title: A finite rectangle cover admits grid control with arbitrarily small volume excess
items.strategy: Enlarge each cube in a given finite cover by a positive margin so that the sum of the enlarged volumes increases by less than a prescribed $\eta$; continuity of the finitely many integer-power volume functions at margin $0$ supplies the choice. Take the minimum of the finitely many positive margins, insert every enlarged-cube endpoint into the corresponding coordinate partition, and pass to a common refinement of mesh below that minimum. Every refined cell meeting the originally covered set then lies inside one of the enlarged cubes. Split the iterated cell sum along the aligned endpoints to bound the total volume of those cells by the sum of the enlarged-cube volumes. Treat closed-cell boundary overlap explicitly. This is the cover-to-grid lemma used twice in the multidimensional Lebesgue criterion.

items.title: Lebesgue's criterion in $\mathbb R^m$: a bounded function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle is Riemann integrable iff its discontinuity set is null
items.strategy: On a closed nondegenerate rectangle, prove sufficiency using compact oscillation superlevels, finite cube covers, grid control, and one uniform mesh on the compact complement. For necessity, a small Darboux gap bounds the total volume of high-oscillation cells. Prove directly that every finite family of axis-parallel rectangles, degenerate ones included, has finite cube covers with total volume arbitrarily close to its rectangle-volume sum, using one common cube side, the integer-part theorem, and polynomial continuity. This converts both the high cells and grid-hyperplane pieces to content-zero covers; countable-union closure then handles the full discontinuity set.

items.title: Jordan inner and outer content and Jordan measurable bounded sets in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: For metric-bounded $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, derive a nondegenerate coordinate bounding box from a Euclidean ball. Define outer content by finite rectangle covers and inner content by finite interior-disjoint inscribed families. The box makes the extrema finite; refining endpoints proves every inner sum is at most every outer sum. Define Jordan measurability by equality and handle empty and degenerate sets explicitly.

items.title: A bounded set is Jordan measurable iff its indicator is Riemann integrable, and the integral is its Jordan content
items.strategy: Choose a nondegenerate bounding rectangle. Indicator lower and upper grid sums are the inner and outer grid approximations. Compare arbitrary finite rectangle approximations with grid approximations by small enlargement or shrinking. Coordinate additivity in a larger rectangle proves that integrability and value are independent of the chosen nondegenerate bound.

items.title: A bounded set in $\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable iff its boundary is null, equivalently of content zero
items.strategy: The indicator of $E$ is discontinuous exactly at $\partial E$. Apply the multidimensional Lebesgue criterion on a nondegenerate bounding rectangle. Metric boundedness supplies a closed bounding box containing $\overline E$; the boundary is closed and therefore compact by Heine-Borel. Compact nullity is equivalent to content zero.

items.title: The Riemann integral of a bounded function over a bounded Jordan measurable set
items.strategy: Let $E$ be metric-bounded and Jordan measurable and $f:E\to\mathbb R$ bounded. Choose a nondegenerate bounding rectangle, extend $f$ by $0$, and define integrability and the integral through that extension. Record bounding-rectangle independence in `justified_by`; for $f=1$ recover Jordan content.

items.title: The Riemann integral over a Jordan set is independent of the bounding rectangle
items.strategy: Place two nondegenerate bounding rectangles strictly inside a larger nondegenerate rectangle. Strict coordinate cuts decompose the larger rectangle into the chosen box and nondegenerate added pieces. Coordinate-slice additivity shows that extending by zero preserves integrability and value, and comparison through the common larger box proves independence.

items.title: A continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set is Riemann integrable over that set
items.strategy: Treat the empty set separately; otherwise the metric extreme-value theorem makes $f$ bounded. In a nondegenerate bounding rectangle the zero extension can be discontinuous only on $\partial E$, which is null by the Jordan criterion. The multidimensional Lebesgue criterion makes the extension integrable.

items.title: Jordan content is finitely additive when the overlap has content zero
items.strategy: For Jordan measurable bounded $E,F$ with $E\cap F$ of content zero, use $1_{E\cup F}=1_E+1_F-1_{E\cap F}$ and multidimensional linearity. The indicator of a content-zero set has integral $0$ by the indicator theorem. State the disjoint case explicitly and obtain finite families by induction, not by a count in prose.

items.title: A Lipschitz map $\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m$ sends null sets to null sets
items.strategy: Cover the null set by cubes. A cube of side $\ell$ has Euclidean diameter at most $\iota(m)\ell$ using the norm comparisons. An $L$-Lipschitz image of it lies in a cube of side $2L\iota(m)\ell$, whose volume is the fixed factor $(2L\iota(m))^m$ times the original volume. Allocate the input cover the corresponding scaled $\varepsilon$ budget and sum. Treat $L=0$ separately. Restrict to equal domain and codomain dimensions; the statement is false across arbitrary dimensions.

items.title: The graph of a continuous function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$ has content zero in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$
items.strategy: Uniform continuity gives a sufficiently fine coordinate grid on the domain for which the vertical oscillation of $f$ on each cell is small. Above each domain cell, stack finitely many $(m+1)$-dimensional cubes whose side is the grid scale; the integer-part lemma bounds the number of cubes by the vertical oscillation divided by that scale plus a fixed endpoint allowance. Summed over the domain grid, their total volume is bounded by a fixed rectangle-dependent constant times the oscillation bound plus the grid scale, and therefore can be made arbitrarily small. This produces the cube covers required by `def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn`, not merely skinny rectangle covers. State $m\geq1$; no metric on $\mathbb R^0$ is needed.

items.title: If every finite interval cover of $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ has total length at least $c$, then every rectangle cover of $A\times[0,d]$ has total area at least $cd$
items.strategy: List a finite rectangle cover and clip it to a bounding rectangle, then partition $[0,d]$ at all listed vertical endpoints. On each resulting horizontal strip, choose an interior height; the horizontal projections of the covering rectangles active there cover $A$, so their widths total at least $c$. Multiply by the strip height and sum. Reindex the resulting nested finite sums using splitting and distributivity. This elementary product estimate supplies the positive-content claim in the compact and open counterexamples without using Fubini or abstract finite-index-set sums.

items.title: Conventions and proved scope for the Riemann integral in $\mathbb R^m$ and Jordan content
items.strategy: Record $m\geq1$, axis-parallel grids, cube covers for nullity, arbitrary finite rectangle covers for Jordan outer content, and both one-dimensional agreement results. State that `thm-lebesgue-criterion-in-rn` uses only cover-nullity and no Lebesgue measure. Record the proved Lipschitz-image theorem. Say only that a continuously differentiable image theorem is not asserted on this page; do not mention an unbuilt total derivative as though it were a dependency.

pages.title: The Riemann Integral in R^m and Jordan Content: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The unit box in $\mathbb R^m$ has volume $1$, and the integral of a constant $c$ over it is $c$
items.strategy: Every side length is $1$, so the finite product volume is $1$, including the indexing check over $j<m$. On every grid, the lower and upper sums of the constant function coincide with $c$ times the sum of cell volumes, hence with $c$. This is a direct computation from the definitions, not an appeal to iterated integration.

items.title: The rational points of $[0,1]^2$ form a bounded null set that is not Jordan measurable
items.strategy: The set $(\mathbb Q\cap[0,1])^2$ is countable, using countability of $\mathbb Q$ and the published pairing of naturals, hence null by the countable-union lemma applied to singleton cubes. Density of the rationals and irrationals in each coordinate makes both the set and its complement dense in the square, so its boundary is the whole square. The unit square is not null, and the Jordan boundary criterion gives non-measurability. This is the bounded plane set without area.

items.title: The Smith–Volterra–Cantor slab $S\times[0,1]$ is compact and not Jordan measurable
items.strategy: The fat Cantor set $S$ is compact, nowhere dense, and every interval cover has total length at least $1/2$. The product slab is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^2$, hence compact, and has empty interior, so it equals its boundary. The product lower-bound lemma gives Jordan outer content at least $1/2$ for that boundary. The boundary criterion therefore rules out Jordan measurability. No product measure or Fubini theorem is used.

items.title: $((0,1)\setminus S)\times(0,1)$ is bounded and open, but its boundary has positive Jordan outer content
items.strategy: The complement of the closed fat Cantor set inside $(0,1)$ is open, so the product is open and bounded. Its boundary contains $S\times[0,1]$ (verify neighbourhood intersections with the open set using nowhere density and with its complement using membership in $S$). Outer-content monotonicity and the slab lower bound give a positive lower bound for the boundary, so the open set is not Jordan measurable.

items.title: The parabola segment $\{(x,x^2):0\leq x\leq1\}$ has content zero in $\mathbb R^2$
items.strategy: Apply the graph theorem to the continuous polynomial $x\mapsto x^2$ on $[0,1]$. Also give the direct uniform-grid estimate: on an interval of width $1/\iota(N)$ the vertical oscillation is at most $2/\iota(N)$, so rectangles covering the graph have total area tending to $0$. Write every reciprocal of a natural through $\iota$.

items.title: The right triangle $\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2:x+y\leq1\}$ has Jordan content $1/2$
items.strategy: Use uniform $N$-by-$N$ grids. Count cells wholly inside and cells meeting the triangle; the two staircase areas differ by at most $1/\iota(N)$ and bracket $1/2$. Prove the finite identity $\sum_{k<N}\iota(k)=\iota(N)\iota(N-1)/2$ by induction or cite a published equivalent only after reading it. The Riemann criterion for the indicator gives Jordan measurability and the common limit $1/2$. The sloping boundary also follows as a graph-content-zero check.

items.title: The Cantor slab $C\times[0,1]$ has content zero in $\mathbb R^2$
items.strategy: Cover the Cantor set by finitely many small intervals. Above an interval of width $\ell>0$, stack finitely many squares of side $\ell$; the integer-part theorem bounds their total area by $\ell+2\ell^2$. Summing gives arbitrarily small finite rectangle covers, so Jordan outer content is zero and the nonnegative inner content is squeezed to zero. Contrast with the fat-Cantor slab.

items.title: The term “rectifiable” for Jordan measurable sets is unrelated to rectifiable curves
items.strategy: Record with a checked Munkres reference that some multivariable-analysis texts call bounded sets with null boundary rectifiable. State the proposition itself: in this page's terminology these are the Jordan measurable bounded sets by the boundary criterion. Warn that this usage does not mean finite curve length and creates no dependency on the arc-length page. Keep the remark terminological and source-backed.

items.title: Transfinite recursion along the ordinals: a class rule determines exactly one operation defined at every ordinal
Ordinal addition exists and is unique: the clauses at $0$, at a successor and at a limit determine one operation, and its values are ordinals
Ordinal addition $\alpha + \beta$
Ordinal multiplication exists and is unique, and its values are ordinals
Ordinal multiplication $\alpha \cdot \beta$
Ordinal exponentiation exists and is unique, with the limit clause taken over $0 < \beta < \lambda$ so that $0^{\lambda} = 0$
Ordinal exponentiation $\alpha^{\beta}$, with the conventions $\alpha^{0} = 1$ and $0^{0} = 1$
$\alpha + \beta$ is the order type of $\alpha$ followed by $\beta$
$\alpha \cdot \beta$ is the order type of $\alpha \times \beta$ ordered by last differences, that is $\beta$ copies of $\alpha$

Monotonicity of ordinal $+$ and $\cdot$: strictly increasing and continuous in the right argument, weakly increasing in the left, with left cancellation, and the identities $0 + \beta = \beta$ and $1 \cdot \beta = \beta$
Ordinal addition is associative
Ordinal multiplication is associative, and $\alpha \cdot (\beta + \gamma) = \alpha\cdot\beta + \alpha\cdot\gamma$
For $\alpha \le \beta$ there is exactly one ordinal $\gamma$ with $\alpha + \gamma = \beta$
For $\alpha > 0$ every ordinal $\beta$ is $\alpha \cdot \xi + \rho$ with $\rho < \alpha$, in exactly one way

$\alpha^{\beta+\gamma} = \alpha^{\beta}\cdot\alpha^{\gamma}$ and $(\alpha^{\beta})^{\gamma} = \alpha^{\beta\cdot\gamma}$; and for $\alpha > 1$ exponentiation is strictly increasing with $\beta \le \alpha^{\beta}$

Cantor normal form: every nonzero ordinal is $\omega^{\beta_0}\cdot c_0 + \cdots + \omega^{\beta_{k-1}}\cdot c_{k-1}$ with $\beta_0 > \cdots > \beta_{k-1}$ and each $c_i$ a nonzero natural number, in exactly one way

On $\omega$ the ordinal $+$ and $\cdot$ are the Peano operations: $\omega$ is closed under ordinal $+$, $\cdot$ and exponentiation, and for naturals $m, n$ the ordinal $m + n$ and $m \cdot n$ are the natural-number sum and product
The first uncountable ordinal $\omega_1 := \aleph(\omega)$
$\omega_1$ is uncountable, every ordinal below it is at most countable, it is a cardinal and a limit ordinal, and its existence is a theorem of ZF
Cofinal subset of an ordinal

Assuming countable choice: every at most countable subset of $\omega_1$ is bounded below $\omega_1$, so no at most countable subset of $\omega_1$ is cofinal in it, and a supremum of at most countably many at most countable ordinals is at most countable
FALSE: ordinal addition is commutative
FALSE: ordinal multiplication is commutative
FALSE: $(\beta + \gamma)\cdot\alpha = \beta\cdot\alpha + \gamma\cdot\alpha$ for all ordinals
FALSE: $\beta < \gamma$ implies $\beta + \alpha < \gamma + \alpha$
FALSE: the ordinal $2^{\omega}$ is uncountable
Ordinal $\alpha^{\beta}$ and cardinal $\kappa^{\lambda}$ are different operations that share one notation
Choice ledger for this page: $\omega_1$ exists in ZF, and the boundedness theorem does not

pages.title: Ordinal Arithmetic and the First Uncountable Ordinal — Examples

items.title: $1 + \omega = \omega$ and $\omega + 1 > \omega$, computed both from the recursion and as order types
$2 \cdot \omega = \omega$ while $\omega \cdot 2 = \omega + \omega$, pictured as order types
$\omega + \omega$ is at most countable although it is not order isomorphic to $\omega$: order type and cardinality are different invariants
$\omega^{2}$, $\omega^{\omega}$, and $\varepsilon_0 = \sup\{\omega, \omega^{\omega}, \omega^{\omega^{\omega}}, \dots\}$ satisfying $\omega^{\varepsilon_0} = \varepsilon_0$
The Cantor normal form of $(\omega^{2} + \omega\cdot 3 + 5) \cdot \omega^{2}$, computed by the division algorithm
Solving $\omega + \gamma = \omega\cdot 2$ and dividing $\omega^{2} + \omega + 3$ by $\omega$
A strictly increasing $\omega$-sequence of countable ordinals has a countable supremum, which is a countable limit ordinal below $\omega_1$
Refuted: every limit ordinal has an at most countable cofinal subset — $\omega_1$ has none, assuming countable choice

pages.title: Cardinal Arithmetic, Cofinality and the Alephs

items.title: A set equinumerous with some ordinal has a least such ordinal, that ordinal is a cardinal, and equinumerous sets get the same one; no choice principle is used

Disjoint union, cartesian product and function space respect equinumerosity, and for cardinals $\kappa, \lambda$ the sets $\kappa \sqcup \lambda$ and $\kappa \times \lambda$ carry explicit well-orders, so their cardinalities exist in ZF
Cardinal sum $\kappa \oplus \lambda$, product $\kappa \otimes \lambda$ and exponentiation $\kappa^{\lambda}$, and why they are written apart from the ordinal operations
Commutativity, associativity, distributivity and monotonicity of $\oplus$ and $\otimes$, the two exponent laws, and $\kappa \le \lambda$ if and only if $\kappa$ injects into $\lambda$
On the natural numbers the cardinal operations are the published finite counting operations, and $\lvert A \rvert$ in the finite sense is $\lvert A \rvert$ in the cardinal sense
$2^{\kappa} = \lvert \mathcal{P}(\kappa) \rvert$, and Cantor's theorem in cardinal form: $\kappa < 2^{\kappa}$
Hessenberg: $\kappa \otimes \kappa = \kappa$ for every infinite cardinal $\kappa$, proved in ZF from the canonical well-order of $\kappa \times \kappa$
Absorption: for cardinals $\kappa, \lambda$ with $\kappa$ infinite and $\lambda \le \kappa$, $\kappa \oplus \lambda = \kappa$, and $\kappa \otimes \lambda = \kappa$ when $\lambda \ne 0$
For every cardinal $\kappa$ the Hartogs number $\aleph(\kappa)$ is the least cardinal strictly above $\kappa$; this is a theorem of ZF

The clauses at $0$, at a successor and at a limit determine exactly one operation $\alpha \mapsto \aleph_\alpha$ and exactly one operation $\alpha \mapsto \beth_\alpha$, each value an infinite cardinal, each strictly increasing and continuous at limits
The successor cardinal $\kappa^{+}$, the alephs $\aleph_\alpha$, the beths $\beth_\alpha$, successor and limit cardinals, and the identifications $\aleph_0 = \omega$ and $\aleph_1 = \omega_1$
Every infinite cardinal is $\aleph_\alpha$ for exactly one ordinal $\alpha$, in ZF; and, assuming the Axiom of Choice, every infinite set is equinumerous with exactly one aleph
Comparability of arbitrary sets, that any two sets admit an injection one way or the other, is equivalent to the Axiom of Choice

Tarski: the Axiom of Choice is equivalent to the statement that $A \times A \approx A$ for every infinite set $A$, so Hessenberg's ZF theorem about alephs does not extend to arbitrary sets without choice
For every ordinal $\alpha$ there is a least ordinal $\beta$ admitting a map $\beta \to \alpha$ with cofinal range, and that map may always be taken strictly increasing
Cofinality $\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)$, and regular and singular cardinals

$\operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \le \alpha$; $\operatorname{cf}(\alpha + 1) = 1$; for a limit ordinal $\lambda$ the value $\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)$ is an infinite cardinal and $\operatorname{cf}(\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)) = \operatorname{cf}(\lambda)$, so it is regular

$\aleph_0$ is regular in ZF; assuming the Axiom of Choice every successor aleph $\aleph_{\alpha+1}$ is regular; $\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_\omega) = \aleph_0$, so $\aleph_\omega$ is singular, and under choice it is the least singular infinite cardinal
The sum $\sum_{i \in I} \kappa_i$ and the product $\prod_{i \in I} \kappa_i$ of an indexed family of cardinals, defined under the Axiom of Choice

K\"onig's theorem: if $\kappa_i < \lambda_i$ for every $i \in I$ then $\sum_{i \in I} \kappa_i < \prod_{i \in I} \lambda_i$; the Axiom of Choice is named in the statement because the theorem implies it
$\kappa < \kappa^{\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)}$ for every infinite cardinal $\kappa$, and $\operatorname{cf}(2^{\kappa}) > \kappa$; in particular $\operatorname{cf}(2^{\aleph_0}) > \aleph_0$
What each result on this page costs in choice, and where the continuum escapes what ZFC can decide
FALSE: $\kappa \oplus \mu = \lambda \oplus \mu$ implies $\kappa = \lambda$
FALSE: $\aleph_\alpha$ is regular for every ordinal $\alpha$
FALSE: $\kappa < \lambda$ implies $\kappa^{\mu} < \lambda^{\mu}$
FALSE: $2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_\omega$

items.title: $\aleph_0 \oplus \aleph_0 = \aleph_0 \otimes \aleph_0 = \aleph_0$, $\aleph_1 \oplus \aleph_0 = \aleph_1$, and $5 \oplus \aleph_0 = \aleph_0$, computed from absorption and from explicit bijections
$\lvert \mathbb{R} \rvert = 2^{\aleph_0}$, by the Cantor set for one injection and by the cuts $\{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q < x\}$ for the other
$\aleph_1 \le 2^{\aleph_0}$ under the Axiom of Choice, and why the inequality is all that ZFC decides
$\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_\omega) = \aleph_0$, computed from the cofinal map $n \mapsto \aleph_n$
$\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_{\omega_1}) = \aleph_1$, so singular does not mean of countable cofinality
An ordinal $\alpha$ with $\aleph_\alpha = \alpha$, built as the supremum of the tower $0, \aleph_0, \aleph_{\aleph_0}, \dots$, and its cofinality is $\aleph_0$
$\beth_0 = \aleph_0$, $\beth_1 = 2^{\aleph_0} = \lvert \mathbb{R} \rvert$, $\beth_2 = \lvert \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}) \rvert$, and $\beth_\omega$ has cofinality $\aleph_0$

pages.title: Topological Spaces and Continuity

items.title: Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison
The discrete, indiscrete, cofinite, cocountable, particular-point and Sierpinski topologies
Basis and subbasis for a topology, and the topology generated by a family of sets

A family is a basis for a unique topology iff it covers the set and every point of an intersection of two members lies in a member inside that intersection; finite intersections of any subbasis form a basis
Neighbourhood of a point and neighbourhood base, with this library’s convention that a neighbourhood need not be open
Interior, closure, boundary, exterior, derived set and isolated point in a topological space
A point lies in the closure of $A$ iff every basic neighbourhood of it meets $A$; the closure is the smallest closed superset and equals $A$ together with its derived set

Interior commutes with finite intersections and closure with finite unions, while the two reverse combinations are inclusions only and both fail for infinite families; the space is the disjoint union of interior, boundary and exterior
Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets
Kuratowski: operators satisfying $c(\varnothing) = \varnothing$, $A \subseteq c(A)$, $c(c(A)) = c(A)$ and $c(A \cup B) = c(A) \cup c(B)$ correspond bijectively to topologies
Continuity of a map of topological spaces at a point and globally

For a map of spaces the following agree: continuity at every point, preimages of open sets open, preimages of closed sets closed, preimages of subbasic open sets open, and $f(\overline{A}) \subseteq \overline{f(A)}$
Subspace topology: the traces of the open sets, its closed sets and its bases, the continuity of the inclusion, and the characteristic property of a map into a subspace
Continuity may be checked on any open cover, and on any finite closed cover; composites of continuous maps are continuous
Homeomorphism, open map, closed map, embedding, and what it means for a property to be topological
A continuous bijection is a homeomorphism iff it is open iff it is closed, and homeomorphy is an equivalence relation on spaces
Convergence and cluster points of a sequence in a topological space, sequential continuity, and the sequential closure
The sequential closure is contained in the closure, continuity implies sequential continuity, and sequential limits need not be unique
First countable space: a countable neighbourhood base at every point
In a first countable space the sequential closure equals the closure and sequential continuity at a point equals continuity there
Metrizable space: a topological space whose topology is induced by some metric; metrizability is topological, the metric is not
FALSE: an arbitrary intersection of open sets is open in every topological space
FALSE: a sequentially continuous map between topological spaces is continuous
FALSE: every continuous bijection of topological spaces is a homeomorphism
FALSE: every topology is induced by some metric
The four live convention forks of general topology and which side this library takes on each

pages.title: Topological Spaces and Continuity: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The discrete and indiscrete topologies, their closures and interiors, and their continuous maps in each direction
On an infinite set the cofinite topology has every infinite subset dense and no two nonempty open sets disjoint
In the cocountable topology on $\mathbb{R}$ the closed sets are the countable sets and $\mathbb{R}$, and a sequence converges iff it is eventually constant
Sierpinski space and the particular-point topology, with their closures and their continuous maps
The order topology on a totally ordered set, with the open rays as a subbasis, and its agreement with the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$

The Sorgenfrey line: $\mathbb{R}$ with the half-open intervals $[a,b)$ as a basis is strictly finer than the usual topology, is first countable and separable, and its sequences converge only from the right
Closure and complement generate at most fourteen sets from any subset, and $(0,1) \cup (1,2) \cup \{3\} \cup ([4,5] \cap \mathbb{Q})$ attains fourteen
In the cocountable topology on $\mathbb{R}$ the sequential closure of $[0,1]$ is $[0,1]$ while its closure is all of $\mathbb{R}$
The identity from the cocountable topology on $\mathbb{R}$ to the usual topology is sequentially continuous and not continuous
In the indiscrete topology every sequence converges to every point, and in the cofinite topology on an infinite set an injective sequence converges to every point
The identity from the discrete topology on $\mathbb{R}$ to the usual topology is a continuous bijection that is not a homeomorphism
$\mathbb{R}$ covered by its closed singletons: every restriction of the indicator of $\{0\}$ is continuous and the map is not, so the closed pasting lemma needs finiteness
In $\mathbb{R}$ the interiors of $\mathbb{Q}$ and of its complement are both empty while the interior of their union is everything
The indiscrete topology on a two-point set is induced by no metric

pages.title: Subspaces, Products, and Quotients

items.title: For $A \subseteq S \subseteq X$ the closure of $A$ in $S$ is $\overline{A}^{X} \cap S$, while the interior only contains $\operatorname{int}^{X}(A) \cap S$, with equality when $S$ is open; and a dense subset of $X$ traces to a dense subset of every open $S$
Hereditary, open-hereditary and closed-hereditary properties of topological spaces

Every subspace of a metrizable space is metrizable and every subspace of a first countable space is first countable, the metric case being the subspace metric already identified with the subspace topology
The initial topology of a family of maps into spaces and the final topology of a family of maps out of spaces, and the subspace topology as the model initial topology

Characteristic properties: a map into a space with the initial topology is continuous iff every composite with the defining family is, a map out of a space with the final topology is continuous iff every composite with the defining family is, and the two topologies are respectively the coarsest and the finest making that family continuous

The product set $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ of functions choosing a point in each factor, the projections, the box topology, and the product topology as the initial topology of the projections; the empty product is a one-point space

A map into a product is continuous iff each of its components is; the projections are continuous and open; and each projection is surjective when every factor is nonempty, which for an infinite index set uses the Axiom of Choice
The box topology is finer than the product topology, the two agree for a finite index set, and the box topology is strictly finer whenever infinitely many factors have a nonempty proper open subset
The product of subspace topologies is the subspace topology of the product, and in the product topology the closure of $\prod A_i$ is $\prod \overline{A_i}$

For $n \ge 1$ the product topology on $n$ copies of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$ is the metric topology of $d_\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and hence also of $d_1$ and $d_2$, so $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a product and $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a metric space are one space
The disjoint union (coproduct) $\bigsqcup_i X_i$ with the final topology of the canonical injections: a set is open exactly when each of its traces is
A map out of a disjoint union is continuous iff each of its restrictions is; the canonical injections are open and closed embeddings; and each summand is clopen in the union
The quotient topology of a surjection, quotient maps, saturated sets, and the quotient of a space by an equivalence relation with its canonical projection

For a quotient map $q : X \to Y$, a map out of $Y$ is continuous iff its composite with $q$ is; a continuous map on $X$ constant on the fibres of $q$ factors uniquely through $q$; and a composite of quotient maps is a quotient map
A continuous open surjection, a continuous closed surjection, and a continuous surjection admitting a continuous section are all quotient maps
Every quotient map $q : X \to Y$ induces a homeomorphism from $X$ modulo the relation "$q$ agrees" onto $Y$, so up to homeomorphism the quotient maps out of $X$ are exactly the canonical projections
The adjunction space $Y \cup_f X$ glued along a continuous map, and the cone and the suspension of a space as quotients of $X \times [0,1]$
Hausdorff space: distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods; every metrizable space is Hausdorff and the indiscrete topology on two points is not
FALSE: the product topology and the box topology agree on every product
FALSE: $\prod_i U_i$ is open in the product topology whenever every $U_i$ is open
FALSE: the projections of a product are closed maps
FALSE: every quotient map is an open map
FALSE: a quotient of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff

What the theory of these constructions still owes at this point in the reading order: preservation of quotient maps under products, separation beyond Hausdorff, and the invariants that tell the glued spaces apart

items.title: $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the product of $n$ copies of the real line: the product topology is the Euclidean topology and the projections are continuous, open and surjective
The hyperbola $\{(x,y) : xy = 1\}$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and its image under the first projection is $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$, which is not closed
The diagonal $x \mapsto (x,x,\dots)$ from $\mathbb{R}$ into $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is continuous for the product topology and not for the box topology
The Cantor set is homeomorphic to $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with the product of discrete topologies, the ternary digits being the coordinates
The Hilbert cube $[0,1]^{\mathbb{N}}$ with the product topology is metrizable, by $d(x,y) = \sum_{k} |x_k - y_k| / 2^{\,k+1}$
$\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$: the quotient map is open, and the quotient is homeomorphic to $[0,1]$ with its endpoints identified
The square with opposite edges identified is homeomorphic to the product $(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}) \times (\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})$
The cylinder and the Mobius band as quotients of the square by $(0,y) \sim (1,y)$ and by $(0,y) \sim (1, 1-y)$, both by a closed quotient map
On $A = ([0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}) \cup (\mathbb{R} \times \{0\})$ the first projection is a quotient map, by the section $x \mapsto (x,0)$, and is neither open nor closed
Two copies of $\mathbb{R}$ glued along $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ give a non-Hausdorff quotient of a metrizable space, by an open quotient map
$\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Q}$ carries the indiscrete topology, although $\mathbb{R}$ is metrizable and the quotient has more than one point
The Sorgenfrey plane: the product of two half-open-interval lines has the rectangles $[a,b) \times [c,d)$ as a basis and $\mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}$ as a countable dense subset
The antidiagonal $\{(x,-x)\}$ is an uncountable discrete subspace of the Sorgenfrey plane, so having a countable dense subset is not a hereditary property

pages.title: Connectedness

items.title: The order topology of a linearly ordered set, with the open rays as a subbasis; order-convex sets, order-density, the least upper bound property, and linear continua
Separation of a topological space, connected and disconnected spaces, clopen sets, and connected subsets
For a topological space the following agree: no separation exists, the only clopen subsets are $\varnothing$ and $X$, and every continuous map to the two-point discrete space is constant
A subspace $A \subseteq X$ is disconnected exactly when $A = A_1 \cup A_2$ with $A_1, A_2$ nonempty and separated in $X$, which is the criterion this library already uses on the real line

The connected subspaces of $\mathbb{R}$ with its usual topology are exactly the order-convex subsets, the published characterisation transported by the identification of the two descriptions of "open in $\mathbb{R}$"
A continuous image of a connected space is connected, and connectedness is a topological property
A real-valued continuous map on a connected space has order-convex image, so it takes every value between any two of its values
A union of connected subspaces with a point in common is connected, and so is a union of a family in which every member meets a fixed connected member
If $A$ is connected and $A \subseteq B \subseteq \overline{A}$ then $B$ is connected; in particular the closure of a connected set is connected
A product of connected spaces is connected in the product topology; for an infinite index set the choice of a base point uses the Axiom of Choice
Connected components, quasicomponents, and totally disconnected spaces
The components of a space are its maximal connected subsets, they partition it, and each of them is closed
Every quasicomponent is a closed union of components, so each component is contained in a quasicomponent; the two need not agree
Paths, path-connected spaces and path components
Locally connected and locally path-connected spaces: a neighbourhood base of connected, respectively path-connected, sets at every point
A space is locally connected exactly when every component of every open subspace is open; in that case the components of the space itself are clopen
Every path-connected space is connected, and every path component lies inside a component
A connected, locally path-connected space is path-connected, because its path components are open
A linear continuum is connected in its order topology, and so is every order-convex subset of it
The closed long ray $\omega_1 \times [0,1)$ under the lexicographic order, and the long line, with the order topology
The long ray is a linear continuum, hence connected; every one of its at most countable subsets is bounded, assuming countable choice

The graph of the piecewise-linear map oscillating between $0$ and $1$ on the intervals $[1/(n+2), 1/(n+1)]$ is path-connected, its closure adds the segment $\{0\} \times [0,1]$, and that closure is connected, not path-connected and not locally connected
Which conventions this page fixes: the empty space and the one-point space, separated sets against disjoint open sets, and what is not developed here
FALSE: every connected topological space is path-connected
FALSE: the closure of a path-connected subspace is path-connected
FALSE: every connected space is locally connected
FALSE: the intersection of two connected subspaces is connected
FALSE: a totally disconnected space carries the discrete topology

pages.title: Connectedness: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Every convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$, in particular every ball and $\mathbb{R}^n$ itself, is path-connected and hence connected
The discrete, indiscrete, cofinite, cocountable, particular-point and Sierpinski topologies placed in the connectedness hierarchy
The zigzag curve and its closure worked out: the components, the path components, and the points at which local connectedness fails
$\mathbb{Q}$ as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}$: every component is a single point, no point is isolated, and the space is not locally connected anywhere
In $\{0,1\} \times \{0\} \cup \bigcup_n \{0,1\} \times \{1/(n+1)\}$ compactified by a limit pair, the quasicomponent of a point is a two-point set while its component is a singleton

pages.title: Compactness

items.title: Open cover, subcover, and compact topological space; a compact subset is a subspace that is compact in its own right
A subspace is compact exactly when every family of open subsets of the ambient space covering it, indexed or not, has finitely many members covering it
For a metric space with its metric topology, compactness in the topological sense is compactness in the published metric sense, and the two notions of compact subset coincide
A space is compact exactly when every family of closed subsets with the finite intersection property has nonempty intersection
A closed subspace of a compact space is compact, and a finite union of compact subspaces is compact

In a Hausdorff space a point and a disjoint compact set, and two disjoint compact sets, have disjoint open neighbourhoods; hence every compact subset is closed, and in a compact Hausdorff space the compact subsets are exactly the closed ones

A continuous image of a compact space is compact; a continuous real-valued map on a nonempty compact space attains a maximum and a minimum; and a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism
Tube lemma: if $K$ is compact and an open $N \subseteq X \times Z$ contains $K \times \{z_0\}$, then $N$ contains $K \times W$ for some open $W \ni z_0$

items.title: $T_0$, $T_1$, and Hausdorffness are hereditary
items.strategy: Intersect the distinguishing or separating open sets with the subspace and use the trace description of closure for the $T_1$ formulation.

items.title: Regularity is hereditary, without a hidden $T_1$ hypothesis

items.title: Complete regularity is hereditary, without a hidden $T_1$ hypothesis

items.title: $T_0$, $T_1$, $T_2$, regularity, $T_3$, complete regularity, and Tychonoffness are hereditary

items.title: Arbitrary products preserve $T_0$, $T_1$, and Hausdorffness

items.title: Arbitrary products of regular spaces are regular

items.title: $T_0$, $T_1$, $T_2$, regularity, $T_3$, complete regularity, and Tychonoffness are productive
items.strategy: Combine the coordinate and finite-support lemmas, again adding $T_1$ only for the named compound axioms.

items.title: Every closed subspace of a normal space is normal
items.strategy: Regard two disjoint closed subsets of the closed subspace as disjoint ambient closed sets and trace ambient separating neighbourhoods.

items.title: A space is completely normal if and only if every subspace is normal
items.strategy: For the forward direction, turn two subspace-closed sets into separated ambient sets and use complete normality. For the reverse direction, place two separated sets in their union, where each is closed, and lift the separating subspace opens.

items.title: Complete normality, and hence $T_5$, is hereditary

items.title: Assuming countable choice, perfect normality, and hence $T_6$, is hereditary

items.title: Every regular Lindelöf space is normal
